questions.stem: A 61-year-old male with longstanding GERD and a history of Barrett’s esophagus undergoes surveillance endoscopy. No mucosal irregularities are seen, but four-quadrant biopsies are obtained of the 2.5 Barrett's segment. Dysplasia is noted on several of the histologic specimens. Which of the following is the next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 61-year-old male with longstanding GERD and a history of Barrett’s esophagus undergoes surveillance endoscopy. No mucosal irregularities are seen, but four-quadrant biopsies are obtained of the 2.5 Barrett's segment. Dysplasia is noted on several of the histologic specimens. Which of the following is the next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: He should continue to undergo surveillance endoscopy to see if this develops into carcinoma.

options.label: B
options.text: He should undergo radiofrequency ablation therapy.

options.label: D
options.text: He should undergo endoscopic mucosal resection

questions.answerText: He should undergo endoscopic mucosal resection
questions.solution: Correct Option D - He should undergo endoscopic mucosal resection: The next step in management in a patient with Barrett's esophagus who is found to have dysplasia within a "short" (<3 cm) Barrett's segment or intramucosal carcinoma in a biopsy, is to perform staging studies (further biopsies, generally at every 1 cm), followed by endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR). Incorrect Options: Option A - He should continue to undergo surveillance endoscopy to see if this develops into carcinoma: This option is incorrect because dysplasia in Barrett's esophagus is considered a precancerous condition. When dysplasia is identified, it indicates an increased risk of developing esophageal carcinoma (cancer). As such, continued surveillance is not the appropriate course of action. Intervention is required to prevent the progression to carcinoma. Option B - He should undergo radiofrequency ablation therapy: This option is incorrect because radiofrequency ablation (RFA) therapy is typically used for the treatment of Barrett's esophagus with low-grade dysplasia or high-grade dysplasia that does not involve any visible cancer (carcinoma in situ). In this case, the patient has dysplasia on several histologic specimens, which may indicate a more advanced stage than what RFA can address. Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or other treatments might be more suitable. Option C - He should undergo photodynamic therapy: This option is incorrect because photodynamic therapy (PDT) is used for treating high-grade dysplasia or early-stage esophageal carcinoma that is limited to the superficial layers of the esophagus (also known as intramucosal carcinoma). In this case, the patient has dysplasia but no visible mucosal irregularities, which suggests that PDT may not be the most appropriate treatment. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents with recurring palpitations, chest pressure, and shortness of breath while walking. He has a 30-year history of heavy alcohol consumption and no significant medical history. Physical exam shows elevated jugular venous pulsations, lung crackles, S3 gallop, and pitting oedema below the knees. The patient's vital signs reveal a pulse of 110/min, blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. What is the best next step in managing the underlying cause of the patient's current condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man presents with recurring palpitations, chest pressure, and shortness of breath while walking. He has a 30-year history of heavy alcohol consumption and no significant medical history. Physical exam shows elevated jugular venous pulsations, lung crackles, S3 gallop, and pitting oedema below the knees. The patient's vital signs reveal a pulse of 110/min, blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. What is the best next step in managing the underlying cause of the patient's current condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Alcohol Abstinence: This patient's history and symptoms point toward diagnosing dilated cardiomyopathy secondary to alcohol usage. The best choice to address the underlying cause of this patient’s clinical condition is to abstain from alcohol given that he has a 30-year history of alcohol consumption. Alcohol is directly toxic to the myocardium and decreases the contractile strength of the heart muscles. It also contributes to the dilation of the ventricles thus leading to dilated cardiomyopathy. If alcohol avoidance is done early, the damage is reversible and the myocardium can resume normal function. Jugular venous distention, lung crackles, S3 gallop and pitting oedema below the knees and tachycardia are common presentations seen in the case of dilated cardiomyopathy. A laterally displaced apical impulse and mitral regurgitation murmur can also be seen in such a case however, these are not reported in this case. Other etiologies of dilated cardiomyopathy include Chagas disease, cocaine use, beriberi, hemochromatosis, titin gene mutation, HIV, and Coxsackie B virus infection. Chronic atrial fibrillation and endocrinopathies like acromegaly, pheochromocytoma and hyperthyroidism are other conditions that result in this disorder. Incorrect Options: Option B- Salt and fluid restriction: These measures may temporarily help improve the symptoms for this patient as he shows signs of volume overload like oedema, jugular venous distention and crackles, but this will not treat the underlying cause of this patient’s condition. Only alcohol abstinence is going to treat the underlying cause. Option C- Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor therapy: An Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor is a first-line medication in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy to improve symptoms. However, this medication does nothing to improve the underlying cause or alter the pathophysiology behind this patient’s issue. Option D-Thiamine Substitution: Thiamine substitution would be beneficial for patients who are suffering from wet beriberi. This patient does not show any symptoms like peripheral neuropathy or confusion. This patient is at risk for B1 deficiency, but that is not the case, as his lack of symptoms shows. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct about SPINK1?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is correct about SPINK1?

options.label: A
options.text: It is considered a susceptibility gene in the development of chronic pancreatitis

questions.solution: Correct Option B - It inhibits trypsin autoactivation: SPINK1 acts as the first line of defense against prematurely activated trypsinogen in the acinar cell and inhibits trypsin autoactivation. It is considered a modifier gene, rather than a susceptibility gene. A mutation affecting SPINK1 does not by itself increase the risk of pancreatic disease. However, in someone with a PRSS1 mutation, the presence of an additional SPINK1 mutation strongly drives the pancreatic injury and resultant fibrosis. CFTR l, not SPINK1, leads to trypsin flushing into the duodenum. CTRC leads to trypsin degradation Incorrect Options: Option A - It is considered a susceptibility gene in the development of chronic pancreatitis: This option is incorrect. In contrast to this statement, Option A is actually correct. SPINK1 gene mutations or variants are considered a susceptibility gene in the development of chronic pancreatitis. Mutations in the SPINK1 gene can lead to reduced inhibition of trypsin, increasing the risk of trypsin activation and autodigestion of the pancreas, which is a key factor in the development of chronic pancreatitis. Option C - It inhibits CFTR: This option is incorrect. SPINK1 does not inhibit CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator). CFTR is a different gene that is associated with cystic fibrosis, a genetic disorder that affects various organs, including the lungs, pancreas, and digestive system. SPINK1 is not directly related to CFTR or cystic fibrosis. Option D - It enhances trypsin degradation: This option is incorrect. SPINK1 inhibits trypsin autoactivation rather than enhancing trypsin degradation. By inhibiting trypsin, SPINK1 helps prevent the premature activation of trypsin in the pancreas, which could lead to pancreatitis. Enhancing trypsin degradation is not one of SPINK1's known functions. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician with complaints of severe eczema, recurrent pyogenic infections, and bleeding episodes. Physical examination reveals eczematous skin lesions, petechiae, and small platelets on peripheral smear. Laboratory tests show low IgG and IgM levels, along with increased IgE and IgA. Which of the following immunodeficiency syndromes is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician with complaints of severe eczema, recurrent pyogenic infections, and bleeding episodes. Physical examination reveals eczematous skin lesions, petechiae, and small platelets on peripheral smear. Laboratory tests show low IgG and IgM levels, along with increased IgE and IgA. Which of the following immunodeficiency syndromes is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome is an X-linked immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the triad of eczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia (low platelet count). Patients with Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome often have bleeding episodes due to the combination of low platelet counts and platelet dysfunction. They also have increased IgE levels, which can contribute to the development of eczema. The syndrome is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome protein (WASP), which plays a crucial role in cytoskeletal organization and immune cell function. Incorrect Options: Option A - X-Linked Bruton's Disease (X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia): X-Linked Bruton’s Disease, also known as X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA), is characterized by a deficiency in B cells and a lack of antibodies (IgG, IgA, and IgM). However, the presentation described in the question includes increased levels of IgE and IgA, which is not consistent with XLA. In XLA, patients would be prone to recurrent bacterial infections but would not have bleeding episodes or increased IgE levels. Option B - X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA): This is not the correct answer for the reasons mentioned above. XLA is characterized by low levels of all immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, and IgM) due to a lack of mature B cells. Option C - Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID): SCID is characterized by severe defects in both T and B cell function, resulting in a profound immunodeficiency. Patients with SCID typically present with severe and recurrent infections from a very young age. The presentation described in the question includes eczema, bleeding episodes, and increased IgE levels, which are not typical of SCID. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 32-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. His heart rate is 180 beats per minute, and his ECG shows narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. He is diagnosed with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Which of the following interventions can be used to terminate this patient’s condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. His heart rate is 180 beats per minute, and his ECG shows narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. He is diagnosed with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Which of the following interventions can be used to terminate this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Valsalva manoeuvre: Vagal manoeuvres are simple techniques used to terminate an episode of PSVT by stimulating the vagus nerve, which slows down the heart rate. These manoeuvres are safe and effective for most patients and can be performed in inpatient and outpatient settings. Some examples of vagal manoeuvres include: Valsalva manoeuvre: This involves forcefully exhaling against a closed airway ( e.g., by pinching the nose and closing the mouth) for 10-15 seconds. This increases intrathoracic pressure , stimulating the vagus nerve and slowing the heart rate. Carotid sinus massage: This involves applying gentle pressure to the carotid artery in the neck for 5-10 seconds. This can activate the baroreceptor reflex, which slows down the heart rate. Cold water immersion of the face involves splashing cold water on the face or immersing the face in cold water for a few seconds. This stimulates the trigeminal nerve, stimulating the vagus nerve and slows the heart rate. Gagging: This involves stimulating the gag reflex by touching the back of the throat with a tongue depressor or toothbrush. This can activate the vagus nerve and slow down the heart rate. Vagal manoeuvres are generally safe, but they should not be performed in patients with certain conditions, such as carotid artery disease, a history of stroke, or glaucoma. Incorrect Options: Option B - Pneumatic compression stockings: Pneumatic compression stockings, also known as compression stockings or compression socks, are commonly used to prevent deep vein thrombosis in hospitalized patients. They work by applying pressure to the legs to improve blood flow. While they can be beneficial for preventing blood clots, they are ineffective in terminating an episode of PSVT. Option C - Oxygen therapy: Oxygen therapy is commonly used in the emergency department to treat hypoxia or respiratory distress. While it can be helpful in certain situations, it is ineffective for terminating an episode of PSVT. Option D - Intravenous fluids: Intravenous fluids may be used in the emergency department to correct hypovolemia or electrolyte imbalances, which can contribute to developing PSVT. However, they are not effective in terminating an episode of PSVT. @Neet_pg_bot

Physical exam shows a warm, firm and tender prostate to palpation. Urine culture has been sent to the lab and is pending. What treatment should be started for initial definitive management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old male comes into the emergency department complaining of malaise, urinary discomfort, and fever with chills. Physical exam shows a warm, firm and tender prostate to palpation. Urine culture has been sent to the lab and is pending. What treatment should be started for initial definitive management of this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Ciprofloxacin 500mg po bid: This patient’s presentation is concerning for acute bacterial prostatitis. The most common organism implicated in prostatitis is Escherichia coli. Initial treatment should be with either a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim sulfa, as these antibiotics are known to have good prostatic penetration. Treatment is generally continued for 6 weeks and should be tailored to the results of the urine culture. Incorrect Options: Option B - Cefazolin 500mg po qid: Cefazolin would not adequately cover this infection. Option C - Valacyclovir 1000mg po tid: Valacylovir is an antiviral medication, which would not cover E. coli. Option D - Ibuprofen 800mg po tid: Ibuprofen can treat the symptoms of malaise and fever, but will not address the infection. @Neet_pg_bot

TIBC (Total Iron Binding Capacity): Elevated TIBC indicates that the body is trying to compensate for low iron levels by increasing its capacity to bind and transport iron. Serum Ferritin: Ferritin is an indicator of the body's iron stores. In this case, the low ferritin level reflects depleted iron stores. Percent Saturation: The percent saturation of transferrin (serum iron/TIBC x 100) is also low due to the insufficient amount of iron available to bind with transferrin. Incorrect Options: Option B - Serum Iron 100 μg/dL, TIBC 420 μg/dL, Serum Ferritin 10 μg/L, Percent Saturation 7%: While the low ferritin and percent saturation are consistent with iron deficiency, a serum iron level of 100 μg/dL is not indicative of iron deficiency anemia, especially considering the low ferritin level and low percent saturation. Iron levels are expected to be low in iron deficiency anemia. Option C - Serum Iron 15 μg/dL, TIBC 420 μg/dL, Serum Ferritin 100 μg/L, Percent Saturation 40%: A serum ferritin level of 100 μg/L is not consistent with iron deficiency anemia. Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and can be elevated in various inflammatory conditions, which would not fit the clinical presentation of this patient with suspected bleeding. Option D - Serum Iron 100 μg/dL, TIBC 325 μg/dL, Serum Ferritin 100 μg/L, Percent Saturation 40%: Similar to the second choice, the high serum iron level is not consistent with iron deficiency anemia due to chronic bleeding. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Oral valganciclovir: Antiviral treatment is indicated for infants with symptomatic congenital CMV infection (generally defined as involvement of at least one end-organ symptom). The treatment of choice for infants with non-life-threatening disease is valganciclovir oral solution. Physical examination findings may include an enlarged thyroid gland, which is typically firm and nontender to palpation. questions.solution: Correct Option A- Chordae tendineae: The chordae tendineae are cord-like tendons that attach to the papillary muscles and the edges of the mitral and tricuspid valves in the heart. They play a crucial role in preventing the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium during systole. In mitral valve prolapse (MVP), the chordae tendineae may be elongated or ruptured , leading to the abnormal bulging of the mitral valve into the left atrium. This can result in mitral regurgitation, which can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath and palpitations, as seen in this patient. Incorrect Options: Option B- Papillary muscles: The papillary muscles are small, cone-shaped muscles that are attached to the chordae tendineae and the ventricular walls. They contract during systole , pulling the chordae tendineae taut and preventing the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium. However, in MVP, the papillary muscles are usually normal and the defect lies in the chordae tendineae. Option C- Tricuspid valve: The tricuspid valve is located between the right atrium and right ventricle , and is not involved in mitral valve prolapse. Option D- Aortic valve: The aortic valve is located between the left ventricle and the aorta , and is not involved in mitral valve prolapse. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Byssinosis: Byssinosis is an occupational lung disease caused by exposure to cotton, flax, and hemp dust. Workers in industries such as cotton mills and textile factories plants are at risk of developing byssinosis. Clinical features of acute byssinosis include the following: Acute byssinosis occurs after short-term exposure to cotton dust and is usually reversible. The symptoms of acute byssinosis typically appear within hours of exposure to cotton dust. Symptoms include cough, wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and fever. These symptoms typically worsen on the first day of work after a period of time off, such as on a Monday after a weekend break, and improve as the week progresses. Clinical features of chronic byssinosis include the following: Long-term exposure to cotton dust leads to chronic byssinosis. The cyclical features of acute byssinosis disappear, and the patient presents with a chronic productive cough. Diagnosis of byssinosis involves: Pulmonary function tests: Decreased FEV1 and normal or increased FEV1/FVC. Chest x-ray: Haziness in the lower lobes of the lungs. Management of byssinosis includes: Avoid exposure to cotton dust Inhaled corticosteroids Bronchodilators Oral corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases Incorrect Options: Option B - Asbestosis: Asbestosis is an interstitial lung disease caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibers. Individuals working in shipbuilding, insulation, roofing, mining, and firefighting equipment manufacturing industries are at risk of inhaling asbestos fibres. Chest x-ray shows pleural plaques and parenchymal infiltrates in the lower lobes of the lung. The textile industry does not expose the individual to asbestos; hence, this diagnosis of asbestosis is less likely. Option C - Silicosis: The inhalation of silica dust in mining, sandblasting, and construction industries is responsible for causing silicosis. Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes and small nodules in the upper lobes of the lung are seen on chest x-ray. This patient is unlikely to be exposed to silica dust while working in the textile industry. Option D - Pneumoconiosis: Exposure to coal dust can cause coal worker’s pneumoconiosis (CWP). CWP is characterised by the accumulation of coal dust particles in the lungs, which can lead to inflammation and fibrosis. Chest x-rays may show small nodules in the upper lobes of the lung. questions.solution: Correct Option D - Confusional arousals – Non-rapid eye movement sleep: Confusional arousals are a disorder of arousal from non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. It occurs typically out of N3 (slow wave) sleep but can also emerge from other NREM stages (N1 or N2). The episodes are characterized by a period of disorientation or confusional behavior and amnesia for the event. During the episode, the individual is less responsive to the environment, and is difficult to awaken. Speech is generally slow and devoid of content. Motor features in confusional arousals are less complex than in other NREM parasomnias such as sleepwalking and sleep terrors, and do not include ambulation (like sleepwalking) or sympathetic activation (like sleep terrors). Incorrect Options: Option A - REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) – N3 sleep: REM sleep behavior disorder is characterized by the loss of muscle atonia during REM sleep, leading to the enactment of dreams. It typically arises from REM sleep, not N3 sleep. Option B - Sleepwalking – Rapid eye movement sleep: Sleepwalking, also known as somnambulism, occurs during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, specifically during N3 sleep, which is the deepest stage of NREM sleep. Option C - Nightmare disorder – Non-rapid eye movement sleep: Nightmares usually occur during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. They are vivid, frightening dreams that can wake a person up from sleep. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Initiation of renal replacement therapy (RRT): The treatment of severe acute kidney injury (AKI) involves aggressive management of the underlying cause and supportive care to maintain vital organ function. The initial management of AKI includes hemodynamic stabilization, which is achieved through fluid resuscitation and correction of electrolyte abnormalities. In cases of severe AKI, renal replacement therapy (RRT) may be required to replace the kidney's filtration function. There are two types of RRT: haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis. Hemodialysis is the most common form of RRT, which involves the use of an external machine to filter blood through a semipermeable membrane. Peritoneal dialysis, on the other hand, involves the installation of a special solution into the abdominal cavity, which helps to remove excess fluid and waste products from the body. In addition to RRT, other treatments may be necessary to manage the underlying cause of AKI. For example, antibiotics may be given for infections, and medication adjustments may be made for patients with drug-induced AKI. Close monitoring and management of complications, such as electrolyte imbalances, acidosis, and fluid overload, are also essential components of the treatment of severe AKI. Incorrect Options: Option A- Administration of a high dose of a loop diuretic: Loop diuretics are commonly used in the management of fluid overload in AKI. However, in cases of severe AKI, where the kidney function is severely compromised, loop diuretics may not be effective in reducing fluid overload. Moreover, high doses of loop diuretics may lead to electrolyte imbalances, such as hypokalemia and hyponatremia. Option C- Empiric antibiotic therapy: Antibiotic therapy is not a standard treatment option for AKI. Although AKI can be caused by infections, such as pyelonephritis or sepsis, antibiotics are only used in these cases. Empiric antibiotic therapy can lead to the development of antibiotic resistance and adverse effects, such as diarrhoea and allergic reactions. Option D- Intravenous infusion of 0.9% saline: Intravenous infusion of 0.9% saline is used in the management of hypovolemia and dehydration. However, in cases of AKI, the administration of 0.9% saline can lead to volume overload and exacerbate the condition. The use of intravenous fluids is guided by the patient's fluid status and electrolyte levels, and excessive fluid administration should be avoided. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) infusion: The clinical presentation of this patient is consistent with pulmonary thromboembolism. Pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) is a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs when a blood clot blocks one or more pulmonary arteries. The clinical presentation of PTE includes dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypoxia. The patient's presentation is a medical emergency and requires prompt diagnosis and management. The most appropriate initial therapy for this patient is tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) infusion. Thrombolysis with tPA is a recommended treatment for patients with PTE who are hemodynamically unstable or have evidence of right ventricular dysfunction. questions.stem: A 50-year-old male patient presented in the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness. The laboratory results revealed low pH, decreased bicarbonate ions, and high potassium. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type 4 is made. Which of the following is the cause of the above-mentioned patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old male patient presented in the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness. The laboratory results revealed low pH, decreased bicarbonate ions, and high potassium. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type 4 is made. Which of the following is the cause of the above-mentioned patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hypoaldosteronism: Hypoaldosteronism is a condition in which there is a deficiency of aldosterone. Normally the activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system leads to the activation of aldosterone. The collecting duct of the nephron is the main site where the aldosterone acts. Normally aldosterone causes the excretion of hydrogen and potassium ions. However, in renal tubular acidosis type 4, there is a deficiency of aldosterone or aldosterone resistance, which results in hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia can be fatal to the heart and can result in life-threatening arrhythmias. With hyperkalemia, ECG changes can occur. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hyperaldosteronism: Hyperaldosteronism is the excessive aldosterone production that results in excessive excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions. As a result, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis is seen in such patients. Option C - ADH deficiency: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) acts on vasopressin receptors that cause the expression of receptors in the distal part of nephrons causing the reabsorption of water. In ADH deficiency, there is insufficient ADH which results in excessive excretion of water leading to decreased urine osmolality and high serum osmolarity. Option D - SIADH: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone is a condition in which there is excessive retention of water due to excess ADH. The urine osmolality is high and there is hypervolemia. Some of the causes of SIADH are meningitis, encephalitis, brain tumors, psychosis, lung disease, etc. @Neet_pg_bot

He was hemodynamically stable on admission but was found to have a Hb of 6.2 g/dL, for which he was transfused 2 units of RBCs in the ER. 20 min into transfusion of the second RBC unit, he develops a fever to 100.9° F with rigors. All other vital signs are completely stable. Physical examination is negative for any acute cardiopulmonary findings or lower extremity edema. After terminating the transfusion, a blood bank work-up was sent, which came out negative for hemolysis, and a clerical check is negative for mistransfusion (i.e., ABO incompatibility between the donor and recipient is ruled out). A bacterial culture of the remaining blood product, which results several days later, is also negative. Which of the following interventions could have prevented this patient’s fever and rigors?

After terminating the transfusion, a blood bank work-up was sent, which came out negative for hemolysis, and a clerical check is negative for mistransfusion (i.e., ABO incompatibility between the donor and recipient is ruled out). A bacterial culture of the remaining blood product, which results several days later, is also negative.
Which of the following interventions could have prevented this patient’s fever and rigors?

options.label: B

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Pre-storage leukoreduction of the blood product
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Pre-storage leukoreduction of the blood product: The clinical history, signs and symptoms are consistent with a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction, which can occur with any blood product (although this reaction most commonly occurs with RBCs and platelets). Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions occur due to the generation and accumulation of cytokines in stored blood products. Therefore, the risk of having a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction positively correlates with increased number of leukocytes in the blood product, as well as the age of the blood product itself. Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions are clinically characterized by the onset of fever (typically 1-2 degrees Celsius increase in body temperature from baseline), chills or rigors that occur 1-6 hours after initiation of the transfusion. A febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction is a diagnosis of exclusion, after other causes of fever in association with a transfusion (such as hemolysis and sepsis) have been ruled out. The primary strategy to prevent the onset of a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction is prestorage leukoreduction of the blood product (answer choice B), which entails passing the cellular blood products through a filter during collection (apheresis) or shortly after collection to remove most of the leukocytes. In addition to reducing the risk of a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction, leukoreduction also decreases the risk of graft rejection in transplant recipients and immune-mediated platelet destruction by minimizing exposure to HLA antigens present on transfused, donor leukocytes. Similarly, leukoreduction also decreases the risk of transfusion-transmitted CMV, as the CMV virus resides within white blood cells. Incorrect Options: Option A - Irradiation of the blood product: Irradiation of blood products causes DNA crosslinks, preventing the replication of lymphocytes without significantly damaging the function of RBCs, platelets or granulocytes. Irradiation of blood products prevents transfusion-associated GVHD in immunosuppressed individuals with deficient cellular immunity and in those receiving blood transfusions from a directed donor (first degree relative donor). Option C - Washing of the blood product: Washing of blood products (answer choice C) removes the plasma component of RBC and platelets. Washing is performed for individuals with IgA deficiency to prevent anaphylactic transfusion reactions mediated by anti-IgA antibodies of the IgE subtype, babies with neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenic purpura (NAIT) to wash out maternal anti-HPA-1a antibodies, and for some individuals with severe allergic transfusion reactions to plasma containing blood products. However, there is no role for washing to prevent the onset of febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions. Option D - Prophylactic administration of acetaminophen prior to initiation of the transfusion: Prophylactic treatment with acetaminophen (answer choice D) is incorrect, as this is not beneficial for preventing febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions. In a double-blinded randomized controlled trial, 315 hematology-oncology patients were randomized to receive either acetaminophen (500 mg) plus diphenhydramine (25 mg) versus placebo 30 minutes prior to transfusion, and monitored for 4 hours. There was no significant difference in the pretreatment and placebo groups with respect to transfusion reactions (1.4 versus 1.5 reactions per 100 transfusions, respectively) (Kennedy et al. Transfusion 2008). Similarly, another review of 6 studies also found no demonstrable benefit of pre-medication with acetaminophen and diphenhydramine to prevent transfusion reactions @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department with acute dyspnoea, wheezing, and chest tightness. She reports a history of asthma and has been non-compliant with her medications. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathology of asthma?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department with acute dyspnoea, wheezing, and chest tightness. She reports a history of asthma and has been non-compliant with her medications. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathology of asthma?

options.label: C
options.text: Inflammatory cell infiltration in alveolar spaces

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy: Bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy is a key feature of the pathophysiology of asthma. In patients with asthma, the bronchial smooth muscle becomes thicker and larger due to hypertrophy and hyperplasia. This leads to increased airway resistance , decreased airflow , and exacerbation of symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath. The smooth muscle hypertrophy in asthma is believed to be due to a combination of chronic inflammation, mechanical stress, and increased responsiveness to growth factors. Inflammation of the airways leads to the release of cytokines and other inflammatory mediators, which stimulate smooth muscle cell proliferation and hypertrophy. Mechanical stress caused by increased airway resistance and stretching of the airways also contributes to smooth muscle hypertrophy. Additionally, asthmatic smooth muscle cells have been shown to be more responsive to growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), which further stimulate hypertrophy and hyperplasia. Incorrect Options: Option B - Alveolar wall thickening: Alveolar wall thickening is a hallmark feature of interstitial lung diseases, such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or sarcoidosis, but not asthma. The thickening of alveolar walls in these conditions can impair gas exchange and lead to progressive lung dysfunction. Option C - Inflammatory cell infiltration in alveolar spaces: Inflammatory cell infiltration in alveolar spaces is not a feature of asthma. While inflammation is a key component of asthma pathophysiology, it occurs primarily in the airway walls and is not typically seen in the alveoli. Option D - Fibrosis of alveolar septa: Fibrosis of alveolar septa is a characteristic finding in conditions such as pulmonary fibrosis, but it is not seen in asthma. Pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive and irreversible lung disease that results in scarring and stiffening of the lung tissue, leading to impaired gas exchange and respiratory failure. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of tumour suppressor genes?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a characteristic of tumour suppressor genes?

options.label: A
options.text: The mutant allele is often inherited through the germ line

options.label: B
options.text: The somatic mutation does not contribute to cancer

options.label: C
options.text: The inherited form of the mutant allele does not commonly have a tissue preference

options.label: D
options.text: The mutant allele acts in a dominant fashion

questions.answerText: The mutant allele is often inherited through the germ line
questions.solution: Correct Option A - The mutant allele is often inherited through the germ line Unlike oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes are commonly inherited through the germ line. The only known example of an oncogene being inherited due to a dominant germline mutation in a proto-oncogene is the RET oncogene, which leads to multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2). Oncogenes act as gain of function mutations and require only one mutation, while tumour suppressor genes generally function as loss of function mutations and require two mutations. Incorrect Options: Option B - The somatic mutation does not contribute to cancer: Somatic mutations in tumor suppressor genes can indeed contribute to cancer development. Somatic mutations are acquired during an individual's lifetime and occur in non-germline cells, such as somatic cells of the body. These mutations can lead to the loss of function of tumor suppressor genes, which, in turn, can result in uncontrolled cell growth and the development of cancer. Inactivation of tumor suppressor genes in somatic cells is a common event in various cancers. Option C - The inherited form of the mutant allele does not commonly have a tissue preference: The inherited form of the mutant allele in some tumor suppressor genes can indeed show a tissue preference or predisposition for specific types of cancer. For example, individuals with germline mutations in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes have a higher risk of developing breast and ovarian cancers. Similarly, individuals with germline mutations in the APC gene have an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer. Option D - The mutant allele acts in a dominant fashion: Tumor suppressor genes typically act in a recessive fashion at the cellular level. This means that both copies (alleles) of the tumor suppressor gene must be inactivated or lost to contribute to the development of cancer. Inherited germline mutations in tumor suppressor genes increase the risk of cancer development, but it usually requires a second "hit" or somatic mutation in the remaining allele to cause complete loss of function and lead to cancer. The loss of both alleles is usually required for the manifestation of malignancy at the cellular level, even though the inheritance pattern at the organismal level may be autosomal dominant. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: For which FIGO stages of ovarian cancer is surgery an appropriate front-line treatment?
questions.stemHtml: For which FIGO stages of ovarian cancer is surgery an appropriate front-line treatment?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- I, II, III, IV: FIGO staging for ovarian cancer is as follows: Stage I: Tumour limited to the ovaries Stage II: Tumour involves one or both ovaries with pelvic extension and/or implants Stage III: Tumour involves one or both ovaries with spread to the peritoneum outside the pelvis or retroperitoneal lymph node metastases Stage IV: Extra-peritoneal distant metastases In patients with FIGO stage III disease, optimal debulking (no macroscopic gross residual disease) improves overall survival outcomes This is reflected in the current NCCN guidelines which recommend surgical debulking for patients with any stage disease who are medically operable and for whom optimal cytoreduction is the likely outcome. Incorrect Options: Option A - I: Surgery is indeed an appropriate front-line treatment for stage I ovarian cancer. In early-stage ovarian cancer, surgery aims to remove the tumor and any involved tissue to achieve complete debulking. Option B - I, II: This option includes stages I and II. Surgery is generally considered the primary treatment approach for both of these early stages of ovarian cancer. Option C - I, II, III: This option includes stages I, II, and III. Surgery is an appropriate front-line treatment for these stages. In cases of stage III ovarian cancer, surgery may involve more extensive procedures to achieve optimal debulking. @Neet_pg_bot

    • Stage IV: Extra-peritoneal distant metastases
  • In patients with FIGO stage III disease, optimal debulking (no macroscopic gross residual disease) improves overall survival outcomes
  • This is reflected in the current NCCN guidelines which recommend surgical debulking for patients with any stage disease who are medically operable and for whom optimal cytoreduction is the likely outcome.

Option C - I, II, III: This option includes stages I, II, and III. Surgery is an appropriate front-line treatment for these stages. In cases of stage III ovarian cancer, surgery may involve more extensive procedures to achieve optimal debulking.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies: The child is suffering from meningitis. Common causes of meningitis in a child is due to Haemophilus influenza, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Among these organisms, the only pleomorphic, gram-negative bacilli is Haemophilus influenzae. Satellitism refers to a phenomenon where one bacterium grows around or near another bacterium, usually relying on the nutrients produced by the other bacterium. Haemophilus influenzae exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies. Haemophilus influenzae requires factors like factor V and factor X produced by Staphylococcus aureus due to hemolysis of the RBCs. Therefore, it grows around the colonies of Staphylococcus aureus on culture media. Incorrect Options: Option A - It is bacitracin sensitive: Bacitracin sensitivity is typically used to differentiate different strains of Streptococcus, particularly in the context of respiratory infections such as pharyngitis. questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option C- Monitoring signs of cerebral edema:

  • In a patient with hypernatremia, sodium concentration is more than 145mEq/L and serum osmolality is greater which causes fluid to shift from the intracellular compartment and cause the cells to shrink
  • Cells adapt to this change in chronic hypernatremia as in the case of elderly patients in which long-standing decreased oral fluid intake cause this hypernatremia
  • When the patient with hypernatremia is treated then these chronic patients should be managed carefully as the rapid correction of hypernatremia in these patient decreases serum osmolality and cause fluid to shift intracellularly and cells swell up
  • This is most important in the brain as it causes cerebral edema and signs and symptoms of neurologic dysfunction
  • Serum sodium should not be decreased by more than 12mEq/L in 24 hours period and 0.5mEq/L per hour
  • So close monitoring of the patient for every 2 to 4 hours for serum sodium and checking for the signs and symptoms of cerebral edema like seizures or any neurologic dysfunction is important

Option A- Monitoring blood glucose level:

  • Monitoring blood glucose levels is important in diabetic patients if they present with high blood glucose levels and positive serum ketones to manage the diabetic ketoacidosis
  • If the blood glucose level is mildly elevated and ketones are negative then blood glucose level monitoring is less important than the management of hypernatremia and its complications in these patients

Option B- Monitoring serum ketones level:

  • Serum ketones are monitored in patients when the presentation is of diabetic ketoacidosis like the fruity smell of the breath, acidic pH, positive serum ketones, and high blood glucose level level
  • If the blood glucose level is normal and ketones are negative then serum ketones monitoring is unnecessary

Option D- Monitoring for urine output:

  • Urine output monitoring is important in severe hypovolemia, decreased blood pressure, and oliguria
  • If the blood pressure and urine output are slightly decreased then monitoring is of secondary importance as compared to monitoring for signs of cerebral edema

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Endoscopic surveillance or endoscopic eradication Both endoscopic surveillance and endoscopic eradication are acceptable management options for low-grade dysplasia in Barrett's Esophagus. Local therapy, if selected, can include photodynamic therapy, spray cryotherapy, endoscopic resection of entire length of Barrett's Esophagus, and radiofrequency ablation (RFA). Endoscopic surveillance, if selected, should be performed every 6 months times 2, then annually unless there is reversion to nondysplastic Barrett's esophagus. Biopsies should be obtained in 4 quadrants every 1 to 2 cm and of any visible lesions. questions.solution: Correct Option C - 52 year old G4P4 female with her son as the platelet donor: Generally, multiparous women are more likely than men or nulliparous women to develop alloimmunization to platelets. Fetal HLA class I antigens inherited from the father are recognized by the mother as foreign. Multiple pregnancies will put the patient at a higher risk of developing such antibodies. Furthermore, receiving a transfusion with her son as the donor greatly increases the risk of re-presenting HLA class I antigens to antibodies which she has developed.Platelet alloimmunization can also occur in patients who have received multiple transfusions or due to antibodies to platelet specific antigens (human platelet antigens). Which of the following adverse effects is most likely to occur?
questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency room for dizziness and palpitations for the past hour. His pulse is 185/min, and his blood pressure is 100/52 mm Hg. An ECG shows a narrow-complex, regular tachycardia without P waves. A drug activates cardiac potassium channels and causes the transient atrioventricular block. Which of the following adverse effects is most likely to occur?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Chest pain: The patient has been given the antiarrhythmic drug adenosine . Chest pain is a common adverse effect in patients treated with adenosine. Adenosine causes a transient atrioventricular (AV) block by increasing potassium efflux from cells, which causes hyperpolarization, decreased calcium influx, and decreased levels of intracellular cAMP. The brief AV block (usually < 15 secs) can cause chest pain and a feeling of impending doom. Other side effects of adenosine include hypotension, flushing, bronchospasm, bradycardia, and nausea. Prolonged asystole is rare but also a potential complication. Theophylline and caffeine are adenosine receptor antagonists that can inhibit the effect of adenosine. Incorrect Options: Option A- Severe headache: This statement is incorrect as severe headache is a common side effect of nitrates (e.g., nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate), which release nitric oxide in smooth muscle cells, resulting in vasodilation and increased intracranial pressure. Other side effects of nitrates include hypotension, reflex tachycardia, and syncope. Severe headaches are not a common side effect of adenosine, which this patient received. Option B- Sedation: This statement is incorrect as sedation is a known side effect of beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol, labetalol) and class IB antiarrhythmics (e.g., lidocaine, mexiletine). These lipophilic agents can penetrate the blood-brain barrier, resulting in CNS side effects. Adenosine does not cause sedation. Option D- Dry cough: This statement is incorrect as adenosine does not cause dry cough. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors can cause dry cough. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Sinding-Larsen-Johansson Disease : This is a condition characterized by traction apophysitis at the inferior pole of the patella. It mainly affects adolescents who are active and involved in sports, particularly those that require repetitive knee movements. The condition arises from stress placed on the patellar tendon as it attaches to the inferior pole of the patella. The repeated stress can lead to inflammation, pain, and tenderness at this site. This condition is similar to Osgood Schlatter disease, which involves the tibial tubercle, but Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease specifically affects the patellar tendon insertion. The patient's symptoms, including tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella and his status as a middle-distance runner, are consistent with this diagnosis. The treatment typically involves relative rest, activity modification, and pain relief measures. The patient in this case, however, has tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella, which is not consistent with Osgood Schlatter disease. Option C - Patello-femoral syndrome: Patellofemoral pain syndrome is a common cause of anterior knee pain. It occurs due to the abnormal tracking of the patella (kneecap) within the femoral groove, leading to pain around or behind the patella. It's often related to activities that involve knee flexion and extension, such as running, squatting, or stair climbing. While patellofemoral syndrome is a possibility, the specific site of tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella and the absence of other relevant symptoms make this diagnosis less likely in the given case. Option D - Sever: Sever's disease, also known as calcaneal apophysitis, is a condition that primarily affects growing adolescents. His jugular vein pressure (also known as JVP) was found to be high throughout the assessment. The JVP rises to a higher level upon inspiration. Which of the following is most likely to explain this finding?
questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man who has a previous medical history of heart failure comes into the emergency department complaining of chest pain and breathlessness. His jugular vein pressure (also known as JVP) was found to be high throughout the assessment. The JVP rises to a higher level upon inspiration. Which of the following is most likely to explain this finding?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Constrictive pericarditis: In a patient who suffers from heart failure, breathlessness, and chest discomfort, constrictive pericarditis is the most likely condition, which is associated with increased jugular venous pressure (JVP) that rises upon inspiration. This finding is known as Kussmaul's sign and is considered pathognomonic for constrictive pericarditis. Constrictive pericarditis is characterized by the thickening and stiffening of the pericardium, the sac-like membrane surrounding the heart. This causes constriction of the heart, leading to impaired diastolic filling and subsequent right-sided heart failure. One of the most common signs of constrictive pericarditis is elevated JVP. There is an increase in venous return during inspiration that contributes to the subsequent rise in JVP that occurs during inspiration. Incorrect Options: Option A- Cardiac tamponade: Cardiac tamponade is characterized by the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac, which can cause heart compression and decrease cardiac output. This can result in symptoms such as shortness of breath, chest pain, and hemodynamic instability. In cardiac tamponade, elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP) is common due to impaired filling and increased central venous pressure. However, unlike in constrictive pericarditis, the JVP typically decreases upon inspiration due to the reduced venous return during inspiration. This finding is known as pulsus paradoxus and a hallmark of cardiac tamponade. Option B- Acute myocardial infarction: Acute myocardial infarction is a life-threatening emergency that happens when a coronary artery suddenly gets blocked, leading to myocardial ischemia and necrosis. The classic symptoms are pain or discomfort in the chest radiating to the jaw or left arm, shortness of breath, sweating, diaphoresis, and nausea or vomiting. Acute myocardial infarction can lead to heart failure, which can cause elevated JVP, but the associated inspiratory increase is not a feature of AMI. Therefore, in the case presented, acute myocardial infarction (B) is not likely to be associated with an elevated JVP that increases upon inspiration. Option C- Pulmonary embolism: PE can cause right-sided heart failure, leading to elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP). However, an elevated JVP that increases upon inspiration is not typically seen in PE. JVP may be normal or even decreased in PE, especially in cases of massive PE. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and confusion. Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals respiratory acidosis. Which of the following structures in the kidney is responsible for regulating acid-base balance?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and confusion. Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals respiratory acidosis. Which of the following structures in the kidney is responsible for regulating acid-base balance?
questions.solution: Option C- Proximal tubule: The kidneys play a key role in regulating the acid-base balance of the body by removing excess acid or base from the blood. The proximal tubule is the primary site of acid-base regulation in the kidney, where bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) are reabsorbed from the filtrate and returned to the bloodstream. Bicarbonate ions are important for buffering acids in the blood and maintaining a pH that is compatible with normal bodily functions. When there is an excess of acid in the blood, such as in the case of respiratory acidosis, the kidneys respond by increasing the reabsorption of bicarbonate ions in the proximal tubule, which helps to neutralise the excess acid and restore the acid-base balance of the body. This process is regulated by several mechanisms, including the action of carbonic anhydrase enzymes in the proximal tubule, which catalyse the conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O) into carbonic acid (H2CO3), which dissociates into bicarbonate ions and hydrogen ions (H+). The hydrogen ions are secreted into the filtrate in exchange for the reabsorption of bicarbonate ions, which are then returned to the bloodstream to help buffer excess acid. Therefore, option C is correct because the proximal tubule is responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Incorrect Options: Option A- Glomerulus: The glomerulus is responsible for filtering blood and removing waste products from the bloodstream, but it is not directly involved in regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. The glomerulus is a network of capillaries in the renal corpuscle that is responsible for filtering blood and producing a filtrate that contains water, electrolytes, and waste products. The filtrate produced by the glomerulus is then modified as it passes through the renal tubules, where various substances are reabsorbed back into the bloodstream or secreted into the urine. While the glomerulus is not directly involved in acid-base regulation, it does play a role in maintaining the electrolyte balance of the body by filtering out excess sodium and other electrolytes from the blood. Therefore, option A is incorrect because the glomerulus is not responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Option B- Bowman's capsule: Bowman's capsule is the cup-shaped structure that surrounds the glomerulus in the renal corpuscle and collects the filtrate that is produced by the glomerulus. While Bowman's capsule is involved in the initial filtration of blood in the kidney, it is not directly involved in the regulation of acid-base balance. Once the filtrate is collected in Bowman's capsule, it then passes into the renal tubules where it is modified and processed. Therefore, option B is incorrect because Bowman's capsule is not responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Option D- Distal tubule: The distal tubule is a part of the renal tubule that comes after the loop of Henle and is responsible for fine-tuning the concentration of urine by reabsorbing some ions and water and secreting others. While the distal tubule plays a role in regulating the balance of electrolytes in the body, it is not primarily responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. The distal tubule does have some capacity to regulate acid-base balance, but its primary function is the regulation of salt and water balance in the body. Therefore, option D is incorrect because the distal tubule is not primarily responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Low serum ceruloplasmin levels: The patient's depression, psychosis (hearing voices), tremor and gait disturbance combined with the characteristic eye finding of Keyser-Fleisher rings, suggests Wilson disease. Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene. ATP7B is a copper-transporting protein that is primarily expressed in the liver, where it facilitates the incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin, a copper-containing protein that is secreted into the blood. Defective ATP7B gene results in defective copper transport and metabolism that leads to copper accumulation in liver leading to cirrhosis. Copper is subsequently deposited in other organs, primarily the basal ganglia in the brain causing neurological dysfunction such as tremors, gait dysfunction, depression and psychosis. Inability of defective ATP7B protein to incorporate copper into apoceruloplasmin leads to low serum ceruloplasmin concentration. Low serum ceruloplasmin is diagnostic for Wilson disease. Incorrect Options: Option A - High serum ferritin: Elevated serum ferritin levels are a common finding in hemochromatosis that can lead to hepatosplenomegaly and signs of liver failure, as well as neurological symptoms if hepatic encephalopathy develops. However, the presence of ascites or peripheral edema would be expected in cases of chronic liver disease. Additionally, hemochromatosis typically presents in patients over 30 years of age and may involve other features, such as skin pigmentation, joint pain, diabetes, and cardiomyopathy and testicular atrophy in males. Option C - Elevated number of CAG repeats: Having an elevated number of CAG repeats on genetic testing is diagnostic of Huntington's disease (HD), which can result in impaired motor abilities such as gait disturbance and tremors. Typical clinical features of HD, including chorea, athetosis, sensory deficits, and autonomic symptoms like sweating and urinary problems, are not present in this patient. Moreover, HD does not affect the liver. Option D - Enlarged ventricles on CT scan of the brain: Enlarged ventricles on brain imaging is indicative of hydrocephalus. Normal pressure hydrocephalus mostly occurs in older individuals and is often associated with difficulty walking. However, since this patient does not exhibit other typical symptoms of NPH like dementia or urinary incontinence, it is less likely to be the underlying cause. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of cellular senescence?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a feature of cellular senescence?

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of ability to secrete tumorigenic growth factors

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Permanent cell cycle arrest Cellular senescence is irreversible cell cycle arrest. Cellular senescence is a programmed cellular response to significant stress. Cells that are in senescence are unable to divide and there are no known physiologic signals that can stimulate senescent cells to proliferate. However, they remain metabolically active and can continue to secrete mitogens that may promote growth of nearby tumour cells. The cellular membrane remains intact and they do not necessarily undergo apoptosis or necrosis. Senescence occurs when cells experience a potentially "oncogenic stress" that could result in progression to malignancy. Thus, it is a mechanism by which cells attempt to prevent carcinogenesis. Examples of causes include depletion of chromosomal telomeres, accumulated DNA damage, or lack of nutrients. It is dependent on activation of the p53 and Rb proteins, which lead to chromatin modifications preventing necessary gene expression for the G1 to S cell cycle transition. Incorrect Options: Option A - Loss of ability to secrete tumorigenic growth factors: This statement is incorrect. Senescent cells can still secrete various factors, including growth factors, cytokines, and proteases, collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Some of these factors may have tumor-promoting effects, which is one of the reasons why senescent cells are implicated in aging and cancer. The SASP can promote inflammation and tissue remodeling, which can contribute to tumorigenesis. Option C - Cessation of all metabolic activity: This statement is incorrect. Cellular senescence is not a state of complete metabolic shutdown. Senescent cells remain metabolically active, and they continue to carry out essential cellular functions, although they are no longer capable of dividing. Option D - Loss of cell membrane integrity: This statement is incorrect. Cellular senescence does not involve the loss of cell membrane integrity. Senescent cells remain intact and viable, although they have permanently stopped dividing. They do not undergo cell lysis or disintegration of the cell membrane. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents to the endocrinology clinic complaining of increased irritability, sensitivity to heat, weight loss, and vibrations. Laboratory tests show an increase in free T4 and a decrease in TSH. Which mechanisms are most likely responsible for the observed changes in this patient's thyroid gland physiology?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old female presents to the endocrinology clinic complaining of increased irritability, sensitivity to heat, weight loss, and vibrations. Laboratory tests show an increase in free T4 and a decrease in TSH. Which mechanisms are most likely responsible for the observed changes in this patient's thyroid gland physiology?

options.label: C
options.text: Ingestion of excessive amounts of dietary iodine

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Autoantibodies against thyroid-stimulating hormone receptors: The patient's clinical features of increased irritability, sensitivity to heat, weight loss, and vibrations suggest hyperthyroidism , which is characterised by increased thyroid hormone production. Autoantibodies against thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH ) receptors are key in developing Graves' disease, the most common cause of hyperthyroidism. These autoantibodies, known as thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI), bind to and activate the TSH receptors on thyroid follicular cells, mimicking the action of TSH. As a result, the thyroid gland produces and releases excessive amounts of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4), leading to the symptoms associated with hyperthyroidism. The binding of TSI to TSH receptors triggers a cascade of events, including increased iodine uptake, thyroid hormone synthesis, and thyroid gland growth. The elevated levels of thyroid hormones in the bloodstream then exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland, suppressing the release of thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) and TSH. This feedback loop results in the decreased TSH levels typically observed in patients with Graves' disease. The clinical manifestations of hyperthyroidism due to Graves' disease include heat intolerance, increased irritability, weight loss, palpitations , and fatigue. Additionally, patients may develop Graves' ophthalmopathy , characterised by exophthalmos (protrusion of the eyeballs), periorbital oedema, and diplopia (double vision). Incorrect Options: Option B - Increased production of thyroxine-binding globulin: Increased thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) production can lead to elevated total T4 levels but would not affect free T4 levels or cause the symptoms described in the scenario. TBG binds to thyroid hormones, reducing their free (biologically active) concentrations. Changes in TBG levels usually have minimal effect on thyroid function. Option C - Ingestion of excessive amounts of dietary iodine: While excessive iodine intake can cause thyroid dysfunction, it typically results in hypothyroidism (reduced thyroid function) rather than the hyperthyroidism observed in this case. The Wolff-Chaikoff effect describes a transient decrease in thyroid hormone synthesis due to high iodine intake, leading to decreased thyroid function. Option D - Dysfunction of the parathyroid glands: Dysfunction of the parathyroid glands can result in abnormal calcium metabolism but does not directly affect thyroid gland physiology. The parathyroid glands produce parathyroid hormone (PTH), which regulates calcium homeostasis, and are not involved in producing or regulating thyroid hormones. @Neet_pg_bot

She is commenced on intravenous antibiotics and fluids.
Which DMARD can continue in a rheumatoid patient with pneumonia?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hydroxychloroquine: The BSR advises holding all synthetic and biological DMARDs in patients with a serious infection except hydroxychloroquine, minocycline and gold. They define a serious infection as one that requires either parenteral antimicrobial therapy or hospital admission. Other synthetic and biological DMARDs can be restarted once the infection has resolved. Incorrect Options: Option A - Adalimumab: Is a tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) inhibitor commonly used as a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) for rheumatoid arthritis. However, TNF-alpha inhibitors can suppress the immune system, potentially increasing the risk of infections. It's generally advisable to hold TNF-alpha inhibitors during acute infections. Option C - Leflunomide: Works by suppressing immune responses. Similar to TNF-alpha inhibitors, continuing leflunomide during an acute pneumonia can potentially weaken the immune response against the infection. Option D - Methotrexate: Is incorrect as like other immunosuppressive drugs, methotrexate is often held during acute infections to avoid further immune suppression, which could hinder the body's ability to fight off the infection. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Chronic alcohol abuse: A known risk factor for the onset of myocarditis is chronic alcohol usage. Alcohol can have toxic effects on the heart muscle, which can result in inflammation and cell damage. Chronic alcohol misuse can also impair immunity, leaving the body more vulnerable to illnesses resulting in myocarditis. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hypertension: A chronic illness known as hypertension causes higher arterial blood pressure. Although many cardiovascular disorders, such as coronary artery disease and heart failure, are at increased risk due to hypertension, myocarditis is not one of them. Option B- Hyperlipidemia: Although hyperlipidemia is not a known risk factor for myocarditis, it is a risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Option D- Diabetes Mellitus: A chronic metabolic condition called diabetes mellitus is characterized by elevated blood sugar levels. Diabetes is an established risk factor for coronary artery disease and heart failure, among other cardiovascular disorders, but it is not one for myocarditis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 62-year-old male presents to the clinic complaining of pain and numbness in his lower legs while walking for a few blocks, which subsides after a few minutes of rest. The patient also reports a history of smoking for the past 40 years and hypertension for the past 15 years, which is currently well-controlled with medication. Physical examination reveals diminished pedal pulses bilaterally, with no signs of peripheral edema or ulceration. The patient denies any symptoms of claudication during a treadmill exercise test. questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old male presents to the clinic complaining of pain and numbness in his lower legs while walking for a few blocks, which subsides after a few minutes of rest. The patient also reports a history of smoking for the past 40 years and hypertension for the past 15 years, which is currently well-controlled with medication. Physical examination reveals diminished pedal pulses bilaterally, with no signs of peripheral edema or ulceration. The patient denies any symptoms of claudication during a treadmill exercise test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Chronic compartment syndrome: Chronic compartment syndrome is a disorder that causes pain and/or neurological problems because of impaired circulation and is characterized by recurring, transient pressure increases inside a fascial compartment. Athletes and military recruits participating in repeated physical exercise are likely to experience it in their lower legs. In this case, the presence of reduced pedal pulses bilaterally and the patient's feelings of discomfort and numbness in the lower legs that go away after a few minutes of rest point to the diagnosis of chronic compartment syndrome. Muscle aches, stiffness, weakness, and swelling are some of the symptoms, which are made worse by exercise and made better by rest. Also possible are paresthesia, numbness, and/or temporary nerve palsy (such as foot drop). The diagnosis is made using invasive compartment pressure measurements taken before and after exercise and symptoms that are consistently triggered by recurrent activity. To assess potential differential diagnoses, noninvasive testing methods including MRI, bone scintigraphy, and radiography may be performed. Conservative management, gait retraining, avoiding stimulating activities, and surgical fasciotomy are all possible forms of treatment. Incorrect Options: Option A- Diabetic neuropathy: Despite the fact that diabetic neuropathy can result in numbness and discomfort in the lower limbs, the patient's history of smoking, high blood pressure, and the presence of reduced pedal pulses on both sides point to a vascular rather than a neuropathic origin. Option B- Sciatica: Sciatica is a condition where the sciatic nerve is strained or irritated. The patient's symptoms are inconsistent with sciatica because they are not back-specific and do not grow worse with spinal movement. Option C- Venous insufficiency: Venous insufficiency can result in leg discomfort, edema, and skin changes; however, the patient's signs of pain and numbness that go away with rest and the existence of reduced pedal pulses on both sides point to an arterial rather than a venous origin. Moreover, venous insufficiency is not frequently diagnosed with a treadmill exercise test. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Infrarenal abdominal aorta: An aortic aneurysm is defined as the dilation of the aortic lumen. The most common site of an aortic aneurysm is the infrarenal abdominal aorta. The shape of the aneurysm is fusiform or saccular, which helps to differentiate it from a false aneurysm . Abdominal aortic aneurysms affect males more commonly than females. It occurs in about 5% of men who are over the age of 60 years. Incorrect Options: Option B- Suprarenal abdominal aorta: An aortic aneurysm can occur above the kidneys and is called a suprarenal aortic aneurysm. A suprarenal aortic aneurysm can affect 10-20% of patients . A suprarenal aortic aneurysm is less common than an infrarenal aortic aneurysm. Option C- Descending thoracic aorta: Aneurysmal dilation of the variable length of the descending aorta can occur in some patients. It can occur in 10-20% of patients with aortic aneurysms. It is not as common as an infrarenal aortic aneurysm. Option D- Ascending thoracic aorta: Aortic aneurysm does not occur commonly in the ascending thoracic aorta. The ascending thoracic aorta is usually spared, and aneurysmal dilation does not occur at this location @Neet_pg_bot

On examination, a prolonged wheeze is appreciated. Spirometry is performed and forced expiratory volume in the first second after the bronchodilator is 65% of the predictive value. A clinical diagnosis of emphysema is made. The patient inquires about the cause of the disease at this young age. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old male presents to the clinic with a complaint of severe shortness of breath. The patient never smoked and is also seeking treatment with a hepatologist for liver issues. On examination, a prolonged wheeze is appreciated. The patient inquires about the cause of the disease at this young age. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor which is synthesised by the liver. It inactivates the neutrophil elastase and protects the lung tissue. It is caused by a genetic mutation which causes a conformational change in the structure of alpha-1 antitrypsin. The dysfunctional protein affects the liver by accumulating in the hepatocytes' endoplasmic reticulum resulting in hepatitis and liver cirrhosis. In the lungs, its deficiency results in an uninhibited activity of neutrophil elastase, which causes pulmonary parenchyma destruction and results in pan acinar emphysema. Patients are < 60 years of age. Incorrect Options: Option B - Smoking Nicotine and smoking cause the inactivation of protease inhibitors and form reactive oxygen species. Smoking results in the destruction of respiratory bronchioles, resulting in centrilobular emphysema. Option C - Bullae formation In giant bullous emphysema, large bullae are formed, which cause the destruction of surrounding pulmonary tissue. Option D - Scar formation The chronic inflammation results in scar formation due to quartz exposure which results in cicatricial emphysema. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old traveler returning from a malaria-endemic region presents with fever, chills, and headache. Blood smear examination reveals ring-shaped parasites within red blood cells. Which stage of the malarial life cycle is primarily responsible for the clinical symptoms in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old traveler returning from a malaria-endemic region presents with fever, chills, and headache. Blood smear examination reveals ring-shaped parasites within red blood cells. Which stage of the malarial life cycle is primarily responsible for the clinical symptoms in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Trophozoite stage: The trophozoite stage of the malarial parasites is responsible for the clinical symptoms of malaria. During this stage, the parasites actively invade and multiply within red blood cells, leading to the characteristic fever, chills, and other systemic manifestations. Incorrect Options: Option A- Sporozoite stage: Sporozoites are the infectious form transmitted to humans by Anopheles mosquitoes. They travel to the liver and undergo maturation, but they do not directly cause clinical symptoms. Option C-Schizont stage: Schizonts are the stage where the parasites mature and divide within the liver cells before releasing merozoites into the bloodstream. While a burst of schizonts can lead to the release of merozoites and subsequent clinical symptoms, it is the trophozoite stage that predominantly causes symptoms within red blood cells. Option D- Gametocytes stage: Gametocytes are the sexual forms of the parasite that are taken up by mosquitoes during a blood meal, contributing to the transmission of malaria. They do not directly cause clinical symptoms in the human host. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Memory B cells: Memory B cells are the correct option based on the immunophenotype described: CD45RO: Memory B cells often express CD45RO, which is a marker associated with memory lymphocytes. Negativity for CD19: Memory B cells typically have lower CD19 expression compared to naive B cells. Negativity for CD37 and CD38: These markers are typically not expressed or are expressed at lower levels on memory B cells. Memory B cells play a crucial role in mounting an efficient immune response upon reexposure to previously encountered pathogens, such as encapsulated bacteria.
