questions.stem: Which of the following symptoms is inconsistent with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following symptoms is inconsistent with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Persistent asymmetry of weakness: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP), or “Guillain-Barre syndrome,” is an autoimmune, areflexic, ascending weakness with mild sensory changes that progresses over a few weeks. It is classically a demyelinating process, although axonal damage may occur in cases of severe demyelination. Predominantly axonal variants also exist (e.g. Miller-Fisher syndrome, acute motor axonal neuropathy). It is often associated with a preceding respiratory infection, gastrointestinal infection, surgery, or vaccination. Characteristic manifestations include: Progressive upper and lower extremity weakness, which may also involve facial, oropharyngeal, and respiratory muscles Areflexia or hyporeflexia Progression over days to weeks (by definition, progression ends by 4 weeks after onset) Symmetry of weakness Mild sensory changes Interscapular or low back pain Cranial nerve palsies (45-75% of cases), often bilateral and involving facial nerves Dysautonomia (e.g. orthostasis, anhidrosis, urinary retention, arrhythmias), occurring in approximately 66% of patients Lack of fever Elevated CSF protein levels persisting beyond the first week of symptoms, in the absence of pleocytosis (”albuminocytological dissociation”) Nerve conduction slowing or blockage on nerve conduction studies Recovery over weeks Findings that are inconsistent with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome include: Persistently asymmetric weakness Clear sensory level Severe bowel or bladder dysfunction at the onset of symptoms A marked CSF pleocytosis should also raise suspicion for an alternative diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Sensory Involvement: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is primarily a motor neuropathy and does not typically involve significant sensory changes. While mild sensory changes may occur in some cases, they are not a prominent feature of GBS. Patients with GBS may experience tingling or mild sensory symptoms, but the hallmark of the condition is progressive weakness rather than sensory deficits. Option C - Cranial Nerve Palsies: Cranial nerve palsies are actually consistent with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome. Approximately 45-75% of GBS cases may involve cranial nerves, often resulting in bilateral facial nerve palsies. Other cranial nerves can also be affected, leading to a variety of cranial nerve-related symptoms such as difficulty swallowing, double vision, or facial weakness. Option D - Dysautonomia: Dysautonomia, which refers to dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system, is a common feature of Guillain-Barre syndrome. About 66% of patients with GBS experience dysautonomia, which may present as symptoms like orthostatic hypotension, changes in heart rate, abnormal sweating patterns, and urinary retention. Dysautonomia is consistent with the demyelinating process affecting the autonomic nerves in GBS. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following interventions/factors has NOT been proven to influence the risk of developing a post-lumbar puncture headache?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following interventions/factors has NOT been proven to influence the risk of developing a post-lumbar puncture headache?

options.label: C
options.text: Replacement of the stylet prior to removal of the needle

options.label: D
options.text: Bevel orientation of a Quincke needle

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Bedrest post-procedure: Despite the common practice of recommending bedrest (“lying flat’) for 30-60 minutes post-procedure, option B is the only factor/intervention of the options listed that hasn’t been shown to have any association with reducing the incidence of post-dural puncture headache (PDPH). Similarly, many of the other factors commonly felt to be associated with an increased risk of a PDPH including patient position, the volume of CSF removed, and the number of attempts made, have also been shown to have no influence on the risk of PDPH. Incorrect Options: Option A - Use of an atraumatic needle: Atraumatic needles, such as Sprotte or Whitacre needles, have a lower risk of causing post-lumbar puncture headaches compared to traditional cutting needles (e.g., Quincke needle). These needles have a rounded tip that separates rather than cuts the dural fibers, reducing the risk of CSF leakage and subsequent headaches. Option C - Replacement of the stylet prior to removal of the needle: Removing the stylet (the inner part of the needle) before removing the needle can create a temporary seal at the puncture site, reducing the risk of CSF leakage and post-lumbar puncture headache. Option D - Bevel orientation of a Quincke needle: The bevel orientation of a Quincke needle (cutting needle) can influence the risk of post-lumbar puncture headache. The bevel orientation should be parallel to the longitudinal axis of the spinal cord, as this reduces the risk of dural fibers being cut and CSF leakage. Option E - Use of a higher gauge (≥ 20 G) needle for the procedure: Smaller gauge needles (e.g., 22 G or 25 G) have been associated with a lower risk of post-lumbar puncture headaches compared to larger gauge needles. The smaller needle size causes less trauma to the dura and reduces the likelihood of CSF leakage. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Perform CT scan of the chest: The clinical scenario presented suggests a diagnosis of pure red cell aplasia (PRCA). PRCA is a condition characterized by a significant reduction in the production of red blood cells without affecting white blood cells and platelets. It often leads to severe anemia. The presence of giant pronormoblasts in the bone marrow biopsy indicates a block in red blood cell maturation at the early stage. One of the potential causes of PRCA is an underlying thymoma, which is a tumor of the thymus gland located in the chest. Thymomas are associated with a paraneoplastic syndrome known as Good syndrome, which can result in PRCA. Therefore, a CT scan of the chest is necessary to assess for the presence of a thymoma. Incorrect Options: Option A - Provide 3 units of packed red blood cells: While transfusing packed red blood cells can help alleviate the anemia temporarily, it does not address the underlying cause of pure red cell aplasia. Treating the underlying cause is essential for long-term management. Option C - Start patient on rituximab: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that targets a specific protein on B cells and is often used in the treatment of certain types of lymphomas and autoimmune disorders. While it can be considered in the treatment of PRCA, it is not the initial step and would not address the need to evaluate for an underlying thymoma. Option D - Start induction chemotherapy with idarubicin and cytarabine: Induction chemotherapy is typically used in the treatment of acute leukemias and other aggressive hematologic malignancies. PRCA is not typically treated with induction chemotherapy unless there are specific indications suggesting a more aggressive disease process, which is not described in this scenario. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A first-time mother presents with her 9-day-old infant who has experienced seizures. The infant had an uncomplicated term delivery and has been otherwise well. The infant has been and remains afebrile. The mother reports diluting the baby's formula. What is the most likely cause of this infant's seizures?
questions.stemHtml: A first-time mother presents with her 9-day-old infant who has experienced seizures. The infant had an uncomplicated term delivery and has been otherwise well. The infant has been and remains afebrile. The mother reports diluting the baby's formula. What is the most likely cause of this infant's seizures?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hyponatremia: In a well newborn without a fever, hyponatremia is the most common cause of seizures. Water intoxication is the most common cause of hyponatremia during infancy. Infants are unable to concentrate urine adequately, so parents who dilute formula or give their infants tap water put their infants at risk. Other causes of neonatal seizures also include neonatal encephalopathy and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, structural brain injuries, including ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke; glucose or other electrolyte abnormalities; and systemic or CNS infections. In a well-baby, a genetic epilepsy syndrome such as benign familial neonatal epilepsy may be the cause. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hypokalemia: Hypokalemia is uncommon in infancy and does not typically cause seizures. Option C - Hypocalcemia: Hypocalcemia is also a common cause of seizures in neonates, so serum calcium levels should be checked. In fact, all infants have a slight decline in serum calcium levels with a nadir at 24 to 48 hours. Symptomatic hypocalcemia is more common in infants of diabetic mothers, preterm infants, or infants with a history of anoxic encephalopathy. Option D - Hypomagnesemia: Hypomagnesemia is not as common as hypocalcemia, but symptoms of hypomagnesemia mimic those of hypocalcemia. It is difficult to correct hypocalcemia if the serum magnesium is also low. Therefore, infants with seizures should have a comprehensive evaluation of their electrolytes. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following would not be associated with a false-positive or false-negative gastric emptying study?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following would not be associated with a false-positive or false-negative gastric emptying study?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Elevated hemoglobin A1c levels: While hyperglycemia at the time of the gastric emptying study can be associated with delayed gastric emptying and a false-positive gastric emptying study, a history of diabetes or an elevated hemoglobin A1c level with a normal blood glucose at the time of the study will not be associated with a false-positive test. Anticholinergic agents such as benztropine will also be associated with a false-positive study. However, domperidone, which is used to stimulate gastric motility (but is not approved for use in the United States), can lead to a false-negative gastric emptying study. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hyperglycemia: Hyperglycemia refers to high blood sugar levels, which can be associated with diabetes. While uncontrolled diabetes can lead to various complications, including gastrointestinal issues, it does not directly impact the results of a gastric emptying study. Hyperglycemia might exacerbate certain gastrointestinal symptoms, but it would not cause false-positive or false-negative results in the study. Option C - Domperidone: Domperidone is a medication used to treat nausea and vomiting. It works by increasing the movement or contractions of the stomach and intestines. If someone is taking domperidone during the gastric emptying study, it might influence the test results by affecting gastric motility. It could lead to false-negative results, where the study may show normal or faster gastric emptying due to the effects of the medication. Option D - Benztropine: Benztropine is an anticholinergic medication used to treat certain movement disorders and side effects of antipsychotic medications. It works by blocking the action of acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter in the nervous system. Anticholinergic drugs can slow down gastrointestinal motility, which could lead to delayed gastric emptying. Therefore, if someone is taking benztropine during the gastric emptying study, it might influence the test results and cause false-positive results, indicating delayed gastric emptying when it's primarily due to the medication's effects. @Neet_pg_bot

His latest laboratory results show an elevated serum potassium level of 5.5 mEq/L. The nephrologist decides to modify his medication regimen to manage his CKD and hyperkalemia. Which of the following drugs is commonly used in the treatment of CKD to reduce proteinuria?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old patient with a history of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and hypertension. His current medications include lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and amlodipine. His latest laboratory results show an elevated serum potassium level of 5.5 mEq/L. The nephrologist decides to modify his medication regimen to manage his CKD and hyperkalemia. Which of the following drugs is commonly used in the treatment of CKD to reduce proteinuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Lisinopril Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor medication that is commonly used in the treatment of CKD. It acts by blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. By inhibiting angiotensin II, lisinopril reduces aldosterone secretion and promotes sodium and water excretion, which can lead to hyperkalemia. Angiotensin II specifically constrict the efferent arteriole and increases the glomerular filtration pressure, and increases the proteinuria. One of the therapeutic effects of ACE inhibitors is reducing proteinuria by dilating the efferent arteriole and thus decreasing the filtration pressure, which ultimately leads to reduced proteinuria, which is a common complication of CKD. Incorrect options: Option B: Hydrochlorothiazide Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic medication that can help reduce blood pressure in patients with hypertension and CKD. It decreases sodium reabsorption and therefore decreases fluid reabsorption; this directly causes decreased levels of circulating sodium. It does not have a significant effect on reducing proteinuria. Option C: Amlodipine Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker medication that can help reduce blood pressure in patients with hypertension and CKD. It does not have a significant effect on reducing proteinuria. Option D: Spironolactone Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic medication that can also reduce blood pressure in patients with CKD. It has no effect on reducing proteinuria. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml:
A three-year-old girl is referred to you for evaluation of several months of progressive gait issues. There is no abnormality on the skin examination over her lumbosacral spine, but imaging reveals a low-lying conus medullaris, consistent with tethered cord syndrome.
Which of the following is an occult spinal dysraphism associated with tethered cord?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Lipomyelomeningocele: Tethered cord syndrome can occur in the setting of both open and occult neural tube defects. Occult spinal dysraphisms have no open defect, but there may be abnormalities of the skin, such as discoloration or a tuft of hair, at the site of the underlying defect. Occult dysraphisms include lipoma, lipomyelomeningocele, dermal sinus, and diastematomyelia (split cord). Open neural tube defects include meningocele (spinal fluid and arachnoid herniate through a dural defect), myelomeningocele (spinal cord tissue, spinal fluid, and arachnoid herniate through defect), hemimyelomeningocele, and myeloschisis (exposed neural tissue without overlying membrane). Incorrect Options: Option A - Hemimyelomeningocele: This is an open neural tube defect where only one half of the spinal cord and its associated structures protrudes through the defect in the vertebral column. It is not associated with occult spinal dysraphism. Option C - Meningocele: This is an open neural tube defect where the spinal fluid and meninges (protective coverings of the spinal cord) herniate through a dural defect. It is not typically associated with tethered cord syndrome. Option D - Myelomeningocele: This is the most severe form of open neural tube defect, where the spinal cord tissue, spinal fluid, and meninges herniate through a defect in the vertebral column. While tethered cord syndrome can develop in individuals with myelomeningocele, the question is specifically asking about an occult spinal dysraphism associated with tethered cord. Myelomeningocele is not an occult condition. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient has a recent history of a family member who had contracted tuberculosis. Which of the following characteristics of the pleural fluid would be characteristic of infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.solution: Correct Options A - Adenosine deaminase (ADA) > 40 U/L: Tuberculosis may present with pleural effusions, which characteristically are composed of a majority of lymphocytes. ADA positivity > 40 U/L makes the infection with tuberculosis more likely, though the finding may be found in malignancies and chronic inflammation. Incorrect Options: Option B - pH < 7.2, lactate dehydrogenase (LD) > 700, and glucose <30: These findings are characteristic of a pleural effusion due to rheumatoid arthritis. These parameters indicate a severe systemic inflammatory response which is not typically associated with tuberculosis. Option C - pH < 6.0: This is an unusually low pH for any type of pleural effusion and is more typically associated with an esophageal perforation leading to the leakage of gastric contents into the pleural space. This is not a typical finding in tuberculosis. Option D - pH < 7.2 with >100,000 neutrophils/mL: This is indicative of a purulent infection, or empyema, in the pleural space. While tuberculosis is an infection, it typically does not cause a purulent effusion and instead leads to a lymphocytic exudative effusion. Therefore, a high neutrophil count is not typically associated with tuberculosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with edema, fatigue, and frothy urine. Blood tests show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Urinalysis shows proteinuria, with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 5. A kidney biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and spike-like projections on silver stain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old female presents with edema, fatigue, and frothy urine. Blood tests show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Urinalysis shows proteinuria, with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 5. A kidney biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and spike-like projections on silver stain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Membranous nephropathy: Membranous nephropathy is a type of glomerulonephritis that affects the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) of the kidneys, leading to proteinuria and often nephrotic syndrome. It is a relatively common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, with an estimated incidence of 2-10 cases per million per year. The diagnosis of membranous nephropathy is typically made based on a combination of clinical presentation, laboratory tests, and kidney biopsy findings. The clinical presentation usually includes edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia. Urine tests will show significant proteinuria, often with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of greater than 3-4. Blood tests may show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Kidney biopsy is necessary to confirm the diagnosis of membranous nephropathy and to distinguish it from other types of glomerulonephritis. The biopsy findings in membranous nephropathy typically show diffuse thickening of the GBM, with subepithelial immune complex deposits that can be seen on electron microscopy. The deposits may appear as spike-like projections or as granular deposits. The glomeruli may also show evidence of mesangial expansion and interstitial fibrosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is classified into three subtypes based on the location of the immune deposits within the glomeruli. These types include: Type I MPGN Type II MPGN (also known as dense deposit disease) Type III MPGN (also known as immune complex-mediated MPGN) Type I MPGN is the most common subtype and is characterized by subendothelial immune deposits, while type II MPGN is characterized by dense intramembranous deposits of complement component C3. Type III MPGN is rare and is characterized by subepithelial or intramembranous immune deposits. Option C - Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a type of acute nephritic syndrome that occurs as a result of an immune response to a group A streptococcal infection, typically a pharyngeal or skin infection. PSGN is more common in children than in adults, and it typically resolves on its own within a few weeks to months. On biopsy, PSGN is characterized by diffuse endocapillary proliferation. There may also be neutrophil infiltration, fibrinoid necrosis, and a "lumpy-bumpy" appearance of the glomeruli due to the deposition of immune complexes. questions.stem: Which of the following parasitic infections is usually associated with occult blood in stool?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following parasitic infections is usually associated with occult blood in stool?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Strongyloides: TRUE: Occult blood in stool is associated with hookworm or Strongyloides infection. Strongyloides stercoralis enters the human host when skin contacts the larvae through infected soil usually contaminated with feces. The parasite can live for up to 5 years in humans, eventually burrowing into the mucosa of the duodenum as adults. Eggs produced by the adult female pass in the feces. Eosinophilia points to a parasite infection. The adult worm migrates to the small bowel and can cause duodenitis, leading to epigastric pain that is aggravated by food ingestion. Patients complain of diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. Pulmonary manifestations can include wheezing, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. questions.stem: A 59 year-old female, with ECOG 1, with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), while screening for dysnea and chest pain was found to have a 4 cm right middle lobe mass, with mediastinal adenopathy, and 2 liver metastases in CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Biopsy demonstrates adenocarcinoma that is consistent with lung origin. Molecular analysis for ROS1, EGFR, and ALK were negative and the PD-L1 proportion score was 4. She was started on first-line chemotherapy with carboplatin, paclitaxel, and bevacizumab. You recommend interval imaging which demonstrates disease progression with 1 new liver metastasis and a new adrenal metastasis. What do you recommend as next step in her management?
questions.stemHtml: A 59 year-old female, with ECOG 1, with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), while screening for dysnea and chest pain was found to have a 4 cm right middle lobe mass, with mediastinal adenopathy, and 2 liver metastases in CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Biopsy demonstrates adenocarcinoma that is consistent with lung origin. Molecular analysis for ROS1, EGFR, and ALK were negative and the PD-L1 proportion score was 4. She was started on first-line chemotherapy with carboplatin, paclitaxel, and bevacizumab. You recommend interval imaging which demonstrates disease progression with 1 new liver metastasis and a new adrenal metastasis. What do you recommend as next step in her management?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Nivolumab: Randomized, phase III data demonstrates an improvement in survival and less toxicity for nivolumab compared to chemotherapy as second-line systemic therapy for patients with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This is true of both squamous and non squamous histologies. Thus, the NCCN Guidelines lists immune checkpoint inhibitors as the preferred choice in this clinical setting. Borghaei et al. performed a randomized, phase III trial in 582 patients with stage IV non squamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who had progressed during or after platinum-based doublet chemotherapy. Patients were randomized to nivolumab (3 mg/kg every 2 weeks) or docetaxel (75 mg/m2 every 3 weeks). The primary end point was overall survival. Nivolumab resulted in improved median overall survival (12.2 vs. 9.4 months, p=0.002), 18-month overall survival (39% vs. 23%), and objective response (19% vs. 12%, p=0.02). Nivolumab resulted in superior outcomes in all groups when divided by programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) proportion score. Furthermore, the nivolumab arm had a lower incidence of grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events (10% vs. 54%). Incorrect Options: Option A - Maintenance bevacizumab: Bevacizumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), a protein that promotes the growth of new blood vessels. In lung cancer, bevacizumab can be used in combination with chemotherapy to inhibit angiogenesis (formation of new blood vessels) and slow down tumor growth. However, in this case, the patient's disease has progressed on the initial regimen, and it's unlikely that continuing bevacizumab alone would be sufficient to control the progression. Option C - Docetaxel: Docetaxel is a chemotherapy drug commonly used to treat various cancers, including NSCLC. It works by disrupting the cell division process in rapidly dividing cancer cells. While docetaxel can be effective in second-line treatment, immune checkpoint inhibitors like nivolumab have shown better outcomes and a more favourable side effect profile in certain patients. Option D - Docetaxel plus ramucirumab: Ramucirumab is another targeted therapy that inhibits angiogenesis by targeting VEGF receptors. It can be combined with chemotherapy like docetaxel for the treatment of certain types of advanced lung cancer. However, given that the patient's disease has progressed after the initial chemotherapy regimen, switching to an immune checkpoint inhibitor like nivolumab might offer a different mechanism of action and potentially better response. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presented to his general practitioner (GP) complaining of increasing dizziness that is aggravated by standing. His general physical and systemic examination was unremarkable and there was no postural hypotension. His medical history included hypertension and type 2 diabetes. His GP requested testing for plasma TSH, ACTH and cortisol levels. Test results revealed: Investigation Result Normal range Serum TSH 2.30 mU/L 0.35-5.5 mU/L Cortisol (8.00 a.m.) 170 nmol/L 180-620 nmol/L Serum ACTH 40 pmol/L 2.2-17.6 pmol/L He was referred to an endocrinologist who ordered a co-syntropin test which showed: Investigation Result Normal range Basal Cortisol (8.10 a.m. 270 nmol/L Post ACTH Cortisol (9.15 a.m.) 624nmol/L >550 Plasma ACTH 40pmol/L 2.2-17.6 What interpretation of the plasma ACTH and co-syntropin test results is correct?

questions.solution: Correct Option A - ACTH assay interference: In an SST, blood is first collected for baseline measurement of plasma cortisol and ACTH level. Then, 250 µg of Synacthen is administered intramuscularly, followed by measurement of cortisol levels at 30 and/or 60 minutes post-Synacthen. The cut-off for a normal cortisol response must be laboratory-specific or assay-specific (ranging from 420 to 574 nmol/L) due to variations among different cortisol assays. In this case, given the high plasma ACTH and borderline low cortisol levels, a short synacthen test (SST) was ordered, which showed normal serum cortisol levels post-Synacthen i.e. >550nmol/L, thereby excluding adrenal insufficiency. In cases of recent onset of secondary adrenal failure up to 4 weeks, it may produce a normal response to an SST but with low ACTH levels. However, in this case, the plasma ACTH that was repeated as part of the SST remained elevated at 40 pmol/L. This discordance between plasma ACTH and SST results should raise suspicion of ACTH assay interference. Measurement of plasma ACTH is an important step in determining the underlying cause of hypercortisolemia. Interfering substances in the immunoassays can lead to erroneous results impacting clinical management and leading to unnecessary investigations and interventions. Many hormones, including ACTH, are measured by immunoassays. The Siemens ACTH immulite assay is widely used in the labs, and has been reported to produce erroneously elevated results. Anything that affects the assay can cause falsely higher or lower results. For example, heterophile antibodies and macro-analyte. Heterophil antibodies are endogenous, weakly reactive antibodies that are found to be in 40% of the general population. A macro-analyte is an analyte bound to an immunoglobulin (e.g. macroprolactin or macro-TSH). It remains in the human circulation longer because of reduced clearance. Macro-analytes are biologically inactive but falsely elevate the result. Communication between physician and laboratory as well as appropriate investigations, including testing on an alternate platform using alternative analyser, serial dilution of sample and use of blocking antibodies, resulted in the identification of assay interference. If the result on an alternative analyser is similar to the initial result, and a serial dilution study shows linearity in the analyte concentrations with increasing dilution, assay interference is unlikely. On the other hand, a different result on an alternative analyser and non-linearity on serial dilution should lead to several more investigations, such as a heterophilic-blocking tube (HBT) study (to exclude heterophile antibodies interference) and a polyethylene glycol precipitation study (to exclude macro-analyte interference). ACTH secreting adenoma (Cushing’s disease), ectopic ACTH syndrome and ectopic CRH secretion are causes of ACTH dependent Cushing’s syndrome in which both ACTH and cortisol levels are high. Random cortisol measurements are unreliable. Highly indicative signs and symptoms such as facial plethora, proximal myopathy, reddish-purple striae, and easy bruisability should alert for biochemical evidence of Cushing’s syndrome through any of the first-line screening tests i.e. 24-hour urinary free cortisol, overnight dexamethasone suppression test, or late-night salivary cortisol. Random cortisol measurements are unreliable. Option C - Ectopic ACTH syndrome: ACTH secreting adenoma (Cushing’s disease), ectopic ACTH syndrome and ectopic CRH secretion are causes of ACTH dependent Cushing’s syndrome in which both ACTH and cortisol levels are high. questions.stem: A 52-year-old G4P4 female with a uT3 uN1b M0 Stage IIIB adenocarcinoma of the proximal rectum required several platelet transfusions during chemotherapy. An interval CECT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrates 3 new liver lesions that are concerning for metastases, requiring biopsy. His pre-procedure CBC reveals a platelet count of 28,000/μL. After 4 units of platelets her platelet count was 33,000/μL. On exam, the patient is well appearing, has no hepatosplenomegaly, and is without evidence of bleeding. Her vitals are stable. Hemoglobin and coagulation profile are within normal limits. What is the best next step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 52-year-old G4P4 female with a uT3 uN1b M0 Stage IIIB adenocarcinoma of the proximal rectum required several platelet transfusions during chemotherapy. An interval CECT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrates 3 new liver lesions that are concerning for metastases, requiring biopsy. His pre-procedure CBC reveals a platelet count of 28,000/μL. After 4 units of platelets her platelet count was 33,000/μL. On exam, the patient is well appearing, has no hepatosplenomegaly, and is without evidence of bleeding. Her vitals are stable. Hemoglobin and coagulation profile are within normal limits. What is the best next step in management?

options.label: B
options.text: Premedicate the patient with corticosteroids and then repeat platelet transfusion

options.label: C
options.text: Test the patient's plasma for antibodies to HLA

options.label: D
options.text: Transfuse the patient with fresh frozen plasma

questions.answerText: Test the patient's plasma for antibodies to HLA
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Test the Patient's Plasma for Antibodies to HLA: Platelet refractoriness occurs when a patient fails to achieve the expected increase in platelet count after platelet transfusion. In this case, the patient's platelet count increased only slightly after receiving 4 units of platelets, which suggests platelet refractoriness. Given the patient's history of multiple pregnancies, there is a higher likelihood of platelet alloimmunization due to antibodies against HLA class I antigens. Testing the patient's plasma for antibodies to HLA is the best next step in management. By identifying the specific antibodies responsible for the refractoriness, it becomes possible to match the patient with HLA-compatible platelet units for future transfusions. Achieving an adequate platelet count is important, especially before a procedure like a liver biopsy (goal platelet count of 50,000/μL). Incorrect Options: Option A - Perform a Bone Marrow Biopsy: A bone marrow biopsy is not necessary in this scenario. The patient's history and clinical presentation strongly suggest platelet refractoriness due to alloimmunization, making testing for HLA antibodies more appropriate. Option B - Premedicate the Patient with Corticosteroids and then Repeat Platelet Transfusion: Corticosteroid premedication is not a common approach for managing platelet refractoriness due to alloimmunization. Identifying the specific antibodies and using HLA-matched platelet units are the primary strategies. Option D - Transfuse the Patient with Fresh Frozen Plasma: Fresh frozen plasma is not indicated for managing platelet refractoriness. It contains clotting factors and is not a standard treatment for addressing the underlying cause of platelet refractoriness, which is the presence of antibodies against HLA antigens. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following does not correspond to brainstem death?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following does not correspond to brainstem death?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Absence of toe jerk: Brain death is when functional brainstem death occurs permanently such that consciousness and spontaneous respiration are impossible . Certain preconditions have to be met for the diagnosis of brain death: The patient must have undergone severe brain damage of known cause Is highly unconscious and unresponsive Requires ventilation No known CNS depressants and muscle relaxants are causing the clinical presentation. Absence of low body temperature, severe hypotension and metabolic or hormonal pathologies With the satisfaction of preconditions, a formal assessment of the brainstem reflexes can be performed. These are to be performed by two clinicians not associated with the transplant team on two separate occasions. The absence of cranial reflexes, motor responses, and spontaneous respiration characterises brain death. An absence of a motor response to painful stimuli to the head/face or within the cranial nerve distribution to adequate stimulation of any somatic area indicates brainstem death. Spinal reflexes such as toe or finger movements do not indicate brainstem death. Incorrect Options: Option A - Absence of pupillary reflex: The absence of cranial nerve reflexes characterises brainstem death. These reflexes are: Pupillary Corneal Gag (pharyngeal) Tracheal (cough) Oculovestibular (caloric) Option B - Absence of spontaneous respiration: The absence of spontaneous respiration characterises brainstem death which is checked in the following manner: Pre Ventilation with 100% oxygen is given for a minimum of 5 minutes. Then, the patient is detached from the ventilator for 10 minutes to confirm the absence of respiration. During this time, the arterial PO 2 must be >8kPa (60 mmHg ) to ensure adequate respiratory stimulation. 6L/min oxygen is delivered through the endotracheal catheter to prevent hypoxia during the apnoea. Option D - Absence of cough: A cough or tracheal reflex is a cranial reflex which characterises brainstem death. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: D

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: This patient presents with acute ST-segment elevation myocardial Infarction (STEMI), which requires immediate reperfusion therapy. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the preferred initial treatment for STEMI when performed within 90 minutes of presentation. PCI involves the insertion of a catheter into the blocked artery to open the occlusion, allowing blood flow to the heart muscle. PCI is more effective than thrombolytic therapy in improving outcomes in STEMI patients. Incorrect Options: Option A- Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery: Coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) is an option for patients with severe and extensive coronary artery disease that cannot be treated with PCI. CABG is not the initial management for acute STEMI and is usually reserved for stable patients with chronic stable angina or unstable angina. Indications of CABG are as follows: High-grade left main stem coronary artery stenosis Significant stenosis (>70%) of the proximal left anterior descending artery, with 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease Symptomatic 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease Disabling angina despite maximal medical therapy Poor left ventricular function with myocardium that can return to function on revascularization Post Infarct angina Indications for emergency CABG Non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction with ongoing ischemia that is unresponsive to medical therapy/PCI STEMI with inadequate response to all nonsurgical therapy Significant ongoing ischemia, traumatic complications, or threatened occlusion in STEMI, after a failed PCI or previous CABG. Option C- Thrombolytic therapy: Thrombolytic therapy involves administering drugs to dissolve the clot causing coronary artery occlusion. Thrombolytic therapy is an alternative to PCI in STEMI patients who present within 12 hours of symptom onset and cannot undergo PCI within 120 minutes. However, thrombolytic therapy has a higher risk of bleeding complications than PCI and is less effective in restoring blood flow to the heart muscle. Option D- Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy: Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is a component of the initial management for STEMI patients but is not the definite treatment for acute STEMI. These medications may stabilize the patient and prevent further clot formation while awaiting PCI or thrombolytic therapy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Beyond genetic testing, which of the following diagnostic tests is often used when considering a diagnosis of Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)?
questions.stemHtml: Beyond genetic testing, which of the following diagnostic tests is often used when considering a diagnosis of Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Skin biopsy: The diagnosis of CADASIL is made with the combination of clinical history, exam, MRI findings, skin biopsy and genetic testing. Although sequencing of the NOTCH3 gene is the gold standard diagnostic test, skin biopsy may also help make the diagnosis due to the involvement of systemic arterioles in addition to the central nervous system vasculature. Electron microscopy of the skin biopsy may show granular osmiophilic material near the basement membrane of arteriole smooth muscle cells. The use of NOTCH3 antibodies may increase the sensitivity of skin biopsy. The other choices have not been systematically assessed for diagnosis of CADASIL and are more invasive and higher risk than skin biopsy. Nonetheless, these changes are present in nerve and muscle tissue as well (see link below) and one could consider evaluating arterioles in these tissues in an individual suspected to have the illness if the tissue is already available for an alternative purpose. Incorrect Options: Option A - Liver biopsy: Liver biopsy is not used for the diagnosis of CADASIL. CADASIL primarily affects the brain and small blood vessels, and liver biopsy is not relevant to this condition. Option C - Muscle biopsy: Muscle biopsy is not a standard diagnostic test for CADASIL. The condition primarily involves the brain's small blood vessels, and muscle biopsy would not provide relevant information for this diagnosis. Option D - Nerve biopsy: Nerve biopsy is not routinely used for the diagnosis of CADASIL. The disease primarily affects the cerebral arteries and small blood vessels in the brain, and nerve biopsy is not a standard procedure for evaluating this condition. @Neet_pg_bot

Which of the following is the underlying acidosis in this patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Accumulation of organic acids Kidneys are the vital organs of the human body that play an important role in the filtration of blood and excretion of metabolic wastes. Kidneys also produce important hormones like vitamin D, erythropoietin, etc. This patient is suffering from metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap. This metabolic acidosis results from the accumulation of organic acids in the body. Some of the causes of renal failure are diabetes, high blood pressure, chronic NSAID users, etc. The accumulation of organic acids is the main reason for the increased anion gap. Some of the symptoms of kidney failure are decreased urine output, fatigue, muscle cramps, fluid overload, nausea, vomiting, dry skin, etc. Incorrect options: Option A: Ketones accumulation Ketone accumulation can also result in an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis but in renal failure, the main cause of metabolic acidosis is the accumulation of organic acids. Ketones are accumulated in the body in diabetes. It is a common condition in type I diabetes mellitus in which insulin is deficient. Option C: Accumulation of salicylates Aspirin is usually used for its analgesic and antiplatelet effect for the management of different diseases. The aspirin is also called salicylates. The salicylate overdose can result in metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap but in renal failure, the main cause of metabolic acidosis is the accumulation of organic acids. It can also cause respiratory alkalosis initially because of the increased respiratory drive. questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old blind patient seeks medical attention for long-standing sleep problems. He has been completely blind since age 32. For the past 10 years, he has suffered from periods of nocturnal insomnia and daytime sleepiness which are very disruptive to his work and family life. In between these periods of insomnia and daytime sleepiness, he may have weeks of near-normal night-time sleep. A 14-day actigraphy record shows a daily delay drift of the onset and offset of the sleep-wake rhythm with a circadian period that is longer than 24 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Non-24-hour sleep wake disorder: The scenario described is typical of non-24-hour sleep wake disorder (N24SWD), formerly known as free-running rhythm disorder, which is characterized by a chronic or recurrent pattern of sleep-wake cycles that are not entrained to the 24-hour environment. questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic complaining of lethargy, malaise, dehydration, and depression that has been worsening for 1 week. She often complains of pain in the right lumbar area. The pain radiates from the loin to the groin. X-ray shows renal stones. Her PTH level is elevated. Which of the following set of biochemical findings correlates with the disease pathology
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Hypophosphatemia, hypercalcemia: Hypophosphatemia and hypercalcemia are the main biochemical findings observed in hyperparathyroidism. The parathyroid hormone is the primary hormone that regulates calcium levels in the body. Hyper parathyroid hormone causes the elevation of calcium levels and decreases the phosphate level . Parathyroid hormone acts on the different parts of the body, which causes the serum calcium levels to increase and serum phosphate levels to decrease in the following ways: Bones It stimulates the osteoblasts at a low serum level, thus building bone. At a higher level, it stimulates osteoclastic activity, thus enhancing bone resorption. Kidney Stimulates 1 alpha-hydroxylase activity . Activates vitamin D. Intestine Increases absorption of both calcium and phosphate. Factors affecting PTH level: Low magnesium elevates PTH Very low magnesium decreases PTH Increased phosphate increases PTH secretion. Low calcium stimulates PTH secretion. Incorrect Options: Option B - Hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia with hyperuricemia: Tumour lysis syndrome occurs when cancer cells break down rapidly, releasing large amounts of intracellular contents into the bloodstream. Lab findings show: Increased potassium levels above 25% from the baseline. Calcium levels al s o decreased by about 25% from the baseline The level of uric acid may also be increased. Option C - Normal phosphate, hypercalcemia: High calcium levels and normal phosphate are seen in the high calcitonin. Option D - Hypernatremia, hypokalemia: Hypernatremia and hypokalemia are seen in Adrenal insufficiency due to a lack of aldosterone and glucocorticoids. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option A - Hypophosphatemia, hypercalcemia:

  • Hypophosphatemia and hypercalcemia are the main biochemical findings observed in hyperparathyroidism.
  • The parathyroid hormone is the primary hormone that regulates calcium levels in the body.
  • Hyper parathyroid hormone causes the elevation of calcium levels and decreases the phosphate level.
  • Parathyroid hormone acts on the different parts of the body, which causes the serum calcium levels to increase and serum phosphate levels to decrease in the following ways:
    • Bones
      • It stimulates the osteoblasts at a low serum level, thus building bone.
      • At a higher level, it stimulates osteoclastic activity, thus enhancing bone resorption.
    • Kidney
      • Stimulates 1 alpha-hydroxylase activity.
      • Activates vitamin D.
    • Intestine
      • Increases absorption of both calcium and phosphate.
  • Factors affecting PTH level:
    • Low magnesium elevates PTH
    • Very low magnesium decreases PTH
    • Increased phosphate increases PTH secretion.
    • Low calcium stimulates PTH secretion.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia with hyperuricemia:

  • Tumour lysis syndrome occurs when cancer cells break down rapidly, releasing large amounts of intracellular contents into the bloodstream.
  • Lab findings show:
    • Increased potassium levels above 25% from the baseline.
    • Calcium levels also decreased by about 25% from the baseline
    • The level of uric acid may also be increased.

Option C - Normal phosphate, hypercalcemia: 

  • High calcium levels and normal phosphate are seen in the high calcitonin.

Option D - Hypernatremia, hypokalemia: 

  • Hypernatremia and hypokalemia are seen in Adrenal insufficiency due to a lack of aldosterone and glucocorticoids.

questions.stem: A mutation in the JAG1 gene is associated with which of the following congenital conditions affecting the biliary tract?
questions.stemHtml: A mutation in the JAG1 gene is associated with which of the following congenital conditions affecting the biliary tract?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Alagille syndrome: Alagille syndrome is characterized by a paucity of interlobular bile ducts. Cholestasis, pulmonic stenosis, dysmorphic facies, butterfly vertebrae, and renal dysplasia are also associated with Alagille syndrome. Patients often have short stature and may have developmental delay. Mutations in the JAG1 gene are associated with more than 90% of cases and are transmitted through autosomal dominant inheritance. Cholestatic liver disease severity is variable, and management may range from conservative treatment for symptoms like pruritus to liver transplantation in 20% of patients who develop end-stage renal disease. Incorrect Options: Option A - Caroli disease: Caroli disease is associated with the PKHD1 gene, which is primarily expressed in the kidneys in addition to the liver, pancreas, and lungs. It is characterized by dilation of intrahepatic bile ducts. Option B - Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2 is the most common type of PFIC and is caused by mutations in ABCB11. Option D - Mirizzi syndrome: Mirizzi syndrome refers to a complication of cholelithiasis in which impaction of a gallstone in the cystic duct causes compression of the common hepatic duct or common bile duct. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: An 8-month-old girl is brought to the paediatric outpatient department by her mother because of bilateral lower limb and abdomen swelling. Physical examination reveals peripheral oedema and hepatomegaly. On auscultation, a loud systolic ejection murmur is heard in the pulmonary area, and the pulmonic component of S2 is not audible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: An 8-month-old girl is brought to the paediatric outpatient department by her mother because of bilateral lower limb and abdomen swelling. Physical examination reveals peripheral oedema and hepatomegaly. On auscultation, a loud systolic ejection murmur is heard in the pulmonary area, and the pulmonic component of S2 is not audible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Pulmonary valve stenosis: The patient presents with the clinical features of Pulmonary valve stenosis. In this condition, the cusps of the pulmonary valve are deformed , and due to this, during systole, the valve does not open completely. An eccentric outlet may occur due to partially fused valve leaflets and, in severe cases, only a central pinhole opening for the outflow. Right ventricular hypertrophy occurs because of increased right ventricular systolic pressure due to obstruction of blood flow from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery. In severe cases, pressure in the right ventricle may be higher than systemic systolic arterial pressure. In neonates, blood can shunt from right to left atrium via foramen ovale in cases of severe pulmonic stenosis as compliance of right ventricle (RV) is decreased, leading to cyanosis. Development and growth are not affected in mild to moderate stenosis. Peripheral oedema, exercise intolerance, hepatomegaly, and signs of right heart failure, develop in severe stenosis. Large presystolic jugular ‘a‘ wave causes venous pressure elevation. RV parasternal lift and cardiomegaly are present. A loud systolic ejection murmur and harshness accompanied by thrill are audible in the pulmonary area. Incorrect Options: Option A- Coarctation of the aorta: The origin of ductus arteriosus below the left subclavian artery origin is the most common site of coarctation of the aorta. It is a feature of the turner syndrome and may occur together with subaortic stenosis and mitral valve abnormalities called Shone complex. Hypoperfusion and rapid deterioration can occur after the ductus arteriosus in neonates who have coarctation. Patients have high blood pressures in the upper limbs and low blood pressure in the lower limbs. Radio-femoral delay is characteristic. A harsh systolic murmur below the left clavicle may be heard. Prostaglandin E1 infusion is given to prevent the closure of the ductus arteriosus. After stabilisation, surgical repair should be performed. As this patient did not have any of these findings, it is an unlikely diagnosis. Option C- Truncus arteriosus: Truncus arteriosus is a condition that occurs due to failure of aorticopulmonary septal development, and a single arterial trunk that arises from the heart supplies systemic and pulmonary circulations. Initial neonatal period findings are cyanosis and murmur. Over the next few months, torrential pulmonary blood flow develops, and heart failure becomes prominent. Single and loud second heart sound is present. As this patient did not have any of these findings, it is an unlikely diagnosis. Option D- Congenital mitral stenosis: Congenital mitral stenosis can occur as an isolated finding or with coarctation of the aorta and aortic stenosis in Shone complex. Dyspnea and failure to thrive occur within the first 2 years in moderate to severe stenosis cases. The left atrium and right ventricle dilate and atrophies leading to cardiomegaly. The second heart sound is loud and split, and an apical rumbling diastolic murmur is an auscultatory finding. As this patient did not have any of these findings, it is an unlikely diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with two days of left calf swelling. An ultrasound confirms the presence of a deep venous thrombosis. Her prior medical history is negative except for 2 miscarriages. Her cousin has systemic lupus erythematosus. She is started on heparin and then blood work is drawn. While awaiting the lab results, you discuss the case with the consulting hematologist, who suspects the patient has antiphospholipid syndrome. What is true about this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman presents with two days of left calf swelling. An ultrasound confirms the presence of a deep venous thrombosis. Her prior medical history is negative except for 2 miscarriages. Her cousin has systemic lupus erythematosus. She is started on heparin and then blood work is drawn. While awaiting the lab results, you discuss the case with the consulting hematologist, who suspects the patient has antiphospholipid syndrome. What is true about this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Antiphospholipid syndrome only occurs concurrently with another autoimmune disorder.

options.label: B
options.text: If the diagnosis is confirmed, the patient’s immediate family members should be tested for antiphospholipid antibodies and, if positive, anticoagulated

options.label: C
options.text: Her obstetrician should have started anticoagulation after the patient had multiple miscarriages

options.label: D
options.text: In addition to blood clots, patients may present with livedo reticularis

questions.answerText: In addition to blood clots, patients may present with livedo reticularis
questions.solution: Correct Option D - In addition to blood clots, patients may present with livedo reticularis: In addition to blood clots, patients with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome may present with livedo reticularis. Livedo reticularis is a condition characterized by a mottled or net-like pattern of reddish or bluish discoloration of the skin. It is often seen in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome and can be associated with the vascular changes caused by the syndrome. Incorrect Options: Option A - Antiphospholipid syndrome only occurs concurrently with another autoimmune disorder: While antiphospholipid is seen more frequently in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) than in the general population -- and can be associated with other autoimmune diseases -- it can also occur as an isolated condition. Option B - If the diagnosis is confirmed, the patient’s immediate family members should be tested for antiphospholipid antibodies and, if positive, anticoagulated: The presence of an antiphospholipid antibody in of itself is not an indication for anticoagulation. Anticoagulation is indicated for patients with antiphospholipid antibodies who have experienced a blood clot. For such patients, lifelong anticoagulation is recommended. Given the current lack of evidence, warfarin should be used over the new generation of anticoagulants. Option C - Her obstetrician should have started anticoagulation after the patient had multiple miscarriages: In patients with obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome -- that is, women diagnosed based upon antibody titers and obstetric complications without a prior blood clot -- there is inadequate data to recommend anticoagulation to prevent the occurrence of the first thrombosis. @Neet_pg_bot

Option A - Antiphospholipid syndrome only occurs concurrently with another autoimmune disorder: While antiphospholipid is seen more frequently in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) than in the general population -- and can be associated with other autoimmune diseases -- it can also occur as an isolated condition.

questions.stem: A 44 year with c/o fatigue of 2 weeks duration, now presents with WBC 3400/µL, Hb 7g/dL and platelet count 25,000 cells/mm3. There are blasts on the peripheral smear, and is diagnosed with IDH1 mutated AML, and starts standard induction chemotherapy. Which of the followed metabolites is a product of this mutated enzyme?
questions.stemHtml: A 44 year with c/o fatigue of 2 weeks duration, now presents with WBC 3400/µL, Hb 7g/dL and platelet count 25,000 cells/mm3. There are blasts on the peripheral smear, and is diagnosed with IDH1 mutated AML, and starts standard induction chemotherapy. Which of the followed metabolites is a product of this mutated enzyme?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- 𝛃 -hydroxy-glutarate: IDH1 (Isocitrate Dehydrogenase 1) is a mutated enzyme that plays a role in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. This enzyme is involved in the conversion of isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate in the TCA cycle. When IDH1 is mutated, it gains a new function: it converts alpha-ketoglutarate into an oncometabolite called D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2HG). D-2HG is an abnormal metabolite that can inhibit various cellular processes and contribute to the development of cancer, including acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Incorrect Options: Option A- Isocitrate: Isocitrate is an intermediate metabolite in the TCA cycle that is converted to alpha-ketoglutarate by the enzyme isocitrate dehydrogenase. IDH1 mutations lead to the production of D-2HG from alpha-ketoglutarate, not isocitrate. Option C- 𝝰-keto-glutarate: Alpha-ketoglutarate is a metabolite in the TCA cycle that is converted to succinyl-CoA. IDH1 mutations lead to the production of D-2HG from alpha-ketoglutarate, but they do not directly affect the production of alpha-ketoglutarate itself. Option D- Succinate: Succinate is another intermediate metabolite in the TCA cycle that is converted to fumarate. IDH1 mutations do not directly influence the production of succinate. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Solitary rectal ulcer: Dyssynergic defecation, mucosal prolapse, and intussusception can result in the uncommon solitary rectal ulcer syndrome (SRUS). Many patients with solitary rectal ulcer syndrome have rectal prolapse and paradoxical contraction of the puborectalis muscle, which causes rectal trauma by forcing prolapsed rectal mucosa downward while the opposing force of the puborectalis generates high pressures in the rectum, leading to mucosal ischemia. Shear forces on the rectal mucosa are also caused by contraction of the puborectalis muscle. Patients may present with straining during defecation, rectal bleeding, and a sense of incomplete evacuation. The syndrome may involve single or multiple ulcers, polypoid or mass lesions, or mucosal erythema. Histologic findings include glandular elongation and fibromuscular obliteration. Management includes observation or treatment with biofeedback and bulk laxatives in asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic patients, with surgery for symptomatic patients who have rectal prolapse or who have severe symptoms that do not respond to conservative management. Incorrect Options: Option A - Lymphoma: Rectal ulceration and proctitis may characterize some cases of infectious proctitis due to lymphogranuloma venereum, secondary syphilis, and amebiasis, but biopsy reveals different features, including acute inflammation in the lamina propria and neutrophilic infiltration of crypts. Option C - Adenocarcinoma of the colon: Although malignancy must be excluded, histologic findings of glandular elongation and fibromuscular obliteration are typical for SRUS. Option D - Ulcerative proctitis: Ulcerative proctitis may appear similar endoscopically to a solitary rectal ulcer. Histologically, inflammation and distortion of the mucosa may suggest inflammatory bowel disease, but the presence of smooth muscle between crypts may help differentiate SRUS. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Somatomedin C Growth hormone is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. It is also known as somatotropin. Its effects are mediated via somatomedins (insulin-like growth factors). The most significant among these is somatomedin C (insulin-like growth factor1). Growth hormone via IGF-1 performs many essential functions in the body, including: Promotion of deposition of protein in the tissues Enhancing utilization of fat for energy Decreasing utilization of carbohydrates Stimulation of growth of cartilage and bones Dwarfism occurs due to deficiency of anterior pituitary hormones. Due to lack of growth hormone, the patient has short stature. Although the body parts develop proportionately to each other but the rate of development is low. The patients also lack sexual maturity due to lack of gonadotrophs. In a specific type of dwarfism known as Levi-Lorain dwarfism , the patients have normal or high growth hormone levels but have a deficiency of somatomedin C (IGF-1) . Due to absent IGF-1 levels, such patients are not able to use growth hormone in their tissues. As a result, they develop signs and symptoms of dwarfism including: Short stature Delayed bone growth Truncal obesity Hypogonadism Blue sclera Depressed nasal bridge Underdeveloped mandible Option A - Growth hormone: Generally, the patients with dwarfism have low levels of growth hormone. questions.answerText: Asbestos exposure increases the risk of lung cancer associated with cigarette smoke exposure
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Asbestos exposure increases the risk of lung cancer associated with cigarette smoke exposure: The risk of lung cancer associated with exposure to both asbestos and cigarette smoke appears to be multiplicative. A 1979 report in the Annals of the New York Academy of Science showed that asbestos is associated with a 6-fold increase, cigarette smoking with an 11-fold increase, and both cigarette smoke and asbestos exposure with a 59-fold increase in the risk of lung cancer. Incorrect Options: Option B - Coughing, sputum production, and wheezing are the most common presenting symptoms: Coughing, sputum production, and wheezing are not the most common presenting symptoms of asbestos-induced lung disease. The most common presenting symptom of asbestos-induced lung disease is dyspnea, which can be a result of interstitial lung disease (asbestosis) or lung cancer. Asbestos exposure primarily affects the lungs' interstitium, leading to fibrosis and scarring, which can cause progressive dyspnea. Option C - Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate have prognostic implications : Antinuclear antibody (ANA), rheumatoid factor (RF), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) are not specific markers for asbestos-induced lung disease. He denies dizziness or syncope. He had a normal colonoscopy 5 months ago. Family history is negative for GI malignancy. On arrival, he is hemodynamically stable. options.label: C

questions.answerText: Focal colitis near the splenic flexure
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Focal colitis near the splenic flexure: Ischemic colitis is the most likely diagnosis in this patient. It commonly occurs in elderly patients who have atherosclerotic disease and is usually found in the area between the distribution of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, near the splenic flexure. Ischemic colitis is the third most common cause of significant bleeding in the lower GI tract. It is generally left-sided and continuous. Findings resemble ulcerative colitis on endoscopy, and bleeding is usually self-limited in contrast to acute mesenteric ischemia of the small intestine. Treatment includes correction of the underlying cause and volume repletion. Incorrect Options: Option A - Multiple colonic polyps: The patient had a normal colonoscopy 5 months ago, so it is unlikely that multiple colonic polyps would have been missed. Option B - Diverticulosis with bleeding diverticulum: Although diverticulosis is the most common source of lower GI bleeding, it is unlikely that diverticulosis would develop so rapidly in light of the normal colonoscopy 5 months ago. Option D - Ulcerative colitis: It is unlikely that the patient has new-onset inflammatory bowel disease. @Neet_pg_bot

Her mother told that she developed an allergic reaction to sulfa antibiotics on her last visit. A voiding cystourethrogram is shown. Which of the following is the mechanism of action for the drug required to prevent long-term complications in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Inhibit cell wall synthesis by blocking peptidoglycan crosslinking

options.label: B
options.text: Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis

options.label: C
options.text: Create free radicals to damage bacterial DNA

questions.answerText: Create free radicals to damage bacterial DNA
questions.solution: Correct Option: C Create free radicals to damage bacterial DNA Nitrofurantoin is used for antibiotic prophylaxis in children >3 months with vesicoureteral reflux who have shown an acute reaction following the administration of sulfonamide antibiotics. Nitrofurantoin is reduced to reactive intermediates by bacterial nitro reductases, which then attack ribosomal proteins, DNA and other molecules within the cell. Adverse effects GI (gastrointestinal) upset Hemolytic anemia in patients with glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency Peripheral neuropathy Liver toxicity Hepatitis Pulmonary fibrosis Contraindications Neonates< 01 month G6PD deficiency Pregnant women at term ( 38 to 42 weeks) During labor and delivery Impaired renal function( creatinine clearance < 60mL/min) Incorrect options: Option A: Inhibit cell wall synthesis by blocking peptidoglycan crosslinking Ampicillin and amoxicillin are less effective as prophylactic agents and are usually reserved for infants < 2 months of age. Option B: Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a folic acid synthesis inhibitor and is used as a drug of choice for prophylactics management in children > 3 months with VUR; however, this patient has shown an allergic reaction following administration of a sulfa-containing antibiotic; therefore the use of TMP-SMZ is contraindicated. Option D: Inhibit 30S subunit of bacterial ribosomes Tetracyclines bind with the 30S subunit of ribosomes and inhibit bacterial protein synthesis. They are not recommended to be used for prophylaxis in children with VUR. They also cause tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Nitrofurantoin is reduced to reactive intermediates by bacterial nitro reductases, which then attack ribosomal proteins, DNA and other molecules within the cell.

Adverse effects

  • GI (gastrointestinal) upset
  • Hemolytic anemia in patients with glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Liver toxicity
  • Hepatitis
  • Pulmonary fibrosis

Contraindications

  • Neonates< 01 month
  • G6PD deficiency
  • Pregnant women at term ( 38 to 42 weeks)
  • During labor and delivery
  • Impaired renal function( creatinine clearance < 60mL/min)

Incorrect options:

Option A: Inhibit cell wall synthesis by blocking peptidoglycan crosslinking

  • Ampicillin and amoxicillin are less effective as prophylactic agents and are usually reserved for infants < 2 months of age.

Option B: Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis

  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a folic acid synthesis inhibitor and is used as a drug of choice for prophylactics management in children > 3 months with VUR; however, this patient has shown an allergic reaction following administration of a sulfa-containing antibiotic; therefore the use of TMP-SMZ is contraindicated.

Option D: Inhibit 30S subunit of bacterial ribosomes

  • Tetracyclines bind with the 30S subunit of ribosomes and inhibit bacterial protein synthesis. They are not recommended to be used for prophylaxis in children with VUR.
  • They also cause tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia.

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Anti-reflux surgery has been shown to improve symptoms in patients with regurgitation: Multiple studies have shown that while anti-reflux surgery does help with symptoms in certain patients, it does not alter an individual’s risk for esophageal cancer. Fundoplication should be reserved for patients with proven regurgitation using esophageal manometry studies. Endoscopic anti-reflux procedures including radiofrequency augmentation of the lower esophageal sphincter and endoscopic suturing of the sphincter have not been proven to result in long-term symptom control. Studies have shown that at 3 years after the procedures, patients continued to need medical therapy or a fundoplication procedure. Anti-reflux surgery is contraindicated in patients with metaplasia or dysplasia since it can affect treatment options in case of progression to cancer. Finally, anti-reflux surgery is associated with worsening of dysphagia in some patients; thus, there is no guarantee that her dysphagia will resolve. It is also associated with gas-bloat syndrome and diarrhea. Incorrect Options : Option A - Anti-reflux surgery will eliminate her risk of esophageal cancer: Anti-reflux surgery can reduce the risk of esophageal cancer by effectively controlling acid reflux and reducing inflammation in the esophagus. However, it does not entirely eliminate the risk of esophageal cancer, especially in patients with a long history of GERD and esophagitis. Option C - Endoluminal antireflux procedures are as effective as anti-reflux surgery without the associated complications of surgery: Endoluminal antireflux procedures, such as endoscopic suturing or radiofrequency ablation, are minimally invasive techniques that aim to improve reflux symptoms. While they may be effective in selected cases, they are generally not considered as effective as traditional anti-reflux surgery (fundoplication) for patients with more severe GERD symptoms or those with anatomical abnormalities like hiatal hernia. Option D - Since she has no evidence of metaplasia or dysplasia on EGD, she is not a candidate for antireflux surgery at this time: The presence or absence of metaplasia or dysplasia (Barrett's esophagus) on EGD (Esophagogastroduodenoscopy) is an important factor in determining the risk of esophageal cancer and the need for surveillance. However, it is not the sole factor in deciding whether a patient is a candidate for antireflux surgery. The decision to proceed with surgery should be based on the severity of symptoms, response to medical therapy, and other factors assessed by the treating physician. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 53-year-old female patient is referred for evaluation of abdominal pain. On examination, several areas of pigmentation are noted on her eyes and lips. EGD reveals pigmented duodenal polyps. Given her suspected diagnosis, she is at risk for several malignancies. At this age, she is at highest risk for developing which of the following malignancies?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Colon cancer: This patient has Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. In Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, the cumulative cancer risk for developing associated cancers increases with age. This risk increases from 2% during the second decade of life to 85% by the seventh decade of life. Regardless of age, patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are at highest risk of developing duodenal and colorectal cancers. This is followed by the risk of breast cancer and then the risk for gynecologic (endometrial and ovarian) cancers. Incorrect Options: Option A - Ovarian cancer: This option is incorrect because the patient's presentation of pigmented duodenal polyps, along with areas of pigmentation on her eyes and lips, suggests a condition known as Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS). Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an inherited disorder characterized by the development of hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract and pigmented macules on the skin and mucous membranes. While individuals with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome do have an increased risk of developing certain malignancies, such as gastrointestinal cancers, ovarian cancer is not typically associated with this syndrome. Therefore, this option is incorrect. Option B - Pancreatic cancer: This option is incorrect because although individuals with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome have an increased risk of developing pancreatic cancer, they are at a higher risk of developing colon cancer. Pancreatic cancer is one of the malignancies associated with PJS, but it is not the highest risk malignancy for individuals with this syndrome. Therefore, this option is incorrect. Option C - Endometrial cancer: This option is incorrect because Peutz-Jeghers syndrome primarily involves the gastrointestinal tract, and while individuals with this syndrome may have an increased risk of developing certain gynecologic cancers, such as cervical cancer, endometrial cancer is not the highest risk malignancy for individuals with PJS. questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician due to a one-month history of weight gain and facial oedema. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, her pulse is 80/min, and her examination shows 2+ ankle oedema. Urine analysis shows 3+ proteinuria and fatty casts. Which of the following is most likely the cause of her proteinuria?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician due to a one-month history of weight gain and facial oedema. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, her pulse is 80/min, and her examination shows 2+ ankle oedema. Urine analysis shows 3+ proteinuria and fatty casts. Which of the following is most likely the cause of her proteinuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Glomerular proteinuria The patient, in this case, has nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome characterized by the following: Proteinuria (> 3-3.5 g/day - most important manifestation) Hypoalbuminemia Edema Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria The basic pathology is the altered permeability of the glomerular membrane for proteins. Diseases most commonly causing nephrotic syndrome are: Minimal change disease (in children) Membranous glomerulopathy (adults) Mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Proteinuria is excessive protein excretion in the urine, generally greater than 150 mg daily in adults. Proteinuria can be associated with high serum creatinine levels, elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) or evidence of systemic illness (e.g., fever, rash, vasculitis). Glomerular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the glomerular filtration barrier in the kidneys. The glomerular filtration barrier is a complex structure comprising three layers: the fenestrated endothelium, the basement membrane, and the podocytes. This barrier is responsible for filtering out waste products and excess fluid from the blood while preventing larger molecules, such as proteins, from entering the urine. Glomerular proteinuria can occur when there is damage or disruption to any of these layers, which can lead to the passage of protein into the urine. It results from the effacement of epithelial cell foot processes and altered glomerular permeability with an increased filtration fraction of normal plasma proteins, as in diabetic nephropathy. Protein electrophoresis will have a pattern exhibiting a large albumin spike indicative of the increased permeability of albumin across the damaged GBM. Incorrect options: Option A: Functional proteinuria Functional proteinuria is not due to any underlying disease or medical condition but a functional body response to certain stressors. This type of proteinuria is usually benign and self-limiting and does not require any specific treatment. Functional proteinuria can be caused by a variety of factors, including: Exercise Fever Emotional stress Dehydration Functional proteinuria is a benign process resulting from acute illness, exercise, and "orthostatic proteinuria." Orthostatic proteinuria usually causes protein excretion of less than 1 g/day. It occurs only during the daytime and is associated with an upright posture. This patient has a history of nephrotic syndrome, so functional proteinuria is unlikely. Option C: Tubular proteinuria Tubular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the reabsorption of proteins by the tubular cells in the kidneys. Normally, the kidney tubular cells reabsorb small amounts of protein that pass through the glomeruli and into the filtrate. However, in tubular proteinuria, there is a defect in the tubular cells that impairs their ability to reabsorb proteins, leading to increased protein levels in the urine. It occurs as the reabsorption of normally filtered proteins in the proximal tubule is defective. It occurs due to a variety of causes: Acute tubular necrosis Toxic injury (lead, aminoglycosides and certain antiretrovirals), Drug-induced interstitial nephritis Hereditary metabolic disorders (Wilson disease and Fanconi syndrome). Option D: Overload proteinuria Overload proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormal blood proteins that exceed the renal tubules' reabsorptive capacity. In this type of proteinuria, the excess protein is not due to a defect in the glomerular filtration barrier or tubular reabsorption but rather due to an excess of abnormal proteins that the renal tubules cannot properly reabsorb. Overload proteinuria can result from: Overproduction of circulating, filterable plasma proteins (monoclonal gammopathies), such as Bence Jones proteins associated with plasma cell myeloma (formerly multiple myeloma). Amyloidosis: Amyloidosis is a condition in which abnormal proteins build up in various tissues in the body, including the kidneys, and can lead to overflow proteinuria. Sickle cell disease: Sickle cell disease can cause the breakdown of red blood cells, releasing hemoglobin into the blood and urine, leading to overflow proteinuria. Fabry disease: It is a genetic disorder in which a buildup of a specific type of fat in the body can produce abnormal proteins that can be excreted in the urine, leading to overflow proteinuria. Protein electrophoresis from the serum or urine will exhibit a discrete protein peak. Other examples of overload proteinuria include myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis and hemoglobinuria in hemolysis. @Neet_pg_bot
