questions.stem: A 58-year-old male with refractory B-cell acute lymphoid leukemia (B-ALL, dx 6 months ago) is currently on ECOG 1910 regimen. He has atrial fibrillation on Lovenox and a history of pulmonary embolism. He is admitted to the ICU with acute neutropenic septic shock secondary to klebsiella bacteremia. There are no other associated symptoms like chest pain, cough, nausea, vomiting, rash, or headache. However, he reports 1-2 days of diarrhea. The decision is made to intubate due to an inability to compensate adequately for severe metabolic acidosis due to suspected gut translocation. Echocardiogram shows mildly dilated LA. LVEF is 60%. He has no valvular abnormalities and normal ventricular contractility. Chest X-ray shows increasing airspace opacities, bilateral lung bases, and midzone alveolar edema. Pneumonia is excluded. The patient has a persistent, small left pleural effusion with associated slight basal atelectasis. Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is considered. As per the Berlin criteria, which oxygenation would label the ARDS as mild?

Compared to the American-European Consensus Conference (AECC definition), the final Berlin definition had better predictive validity for mortality. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Male donor for female recipient: Chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD) is a complex and multifactorial condition that can develop after allogeneic stem cell transplantation. While the development of cGVHD is influenced by various factors, including the patient's underlying disease, the conditioning regimen, and the immune system's interaction between the donor and recipient, there is no known direct correlation between the sex (gender) of the donor and recipient and the risk of cGVHD. Therefore, having a male donor for a female recipient is not considered a risk factor for the development of cGVHD. Incorrect Options: Option A - Older age of recipient: Older age of the transplant recipient is a well-established risk factor for the development of cGVHD. Older recipients are generally more prone to cGVHD, and the incidence tends to increase with advancing age. Option C - Higher degree of HLA mismatching: HLA mismatching between the donor and recipient is a significant risk factor for both acute and chronic GVHD. A higher degree of HLA mismatching is associated with an increased risk of cGVHD. Option D - Peripheral blood stem cell rather than bone marrow or umbilical cord: The source of stem cells can influence the risk of cGVHD. Peripheral blood stem cell (PBSC) transplants are associated with a higher risk of cGVHD compared to bone marrow or umbilical cord blood transplants. The reasons for this difference include the greater number of immune cells in PBSC grafts and the different composition of immune cells in PBSCs compared to bone marrow or cord blood. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: B

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Surgical bypass of the annular ring
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Surgical bypass of the annular ring: Annular pancreas is a congenital abnormality of the pancreas defined by a ring of pancreatic tissue encapsulating the descending portion of the duodenum, most likely due to incomplete rotation of the embryologic ventral pancreatic bud. Since it is usually asymptomatic, the incidence is unknown, but it appears to occur rarely. It is characterized as complete or incomplete and classified into subtypes based upon the drainage of the annular duct. Symptoms may occur as early as the neonatal period, but age of onset is determined by severity of obstruction. Typically, adults present between the ages of 20 and 50 with chronic abdominal pain, early satiety, nausea, and vomiting. Performance of cholangiopancreatogram allows delineation of the structure of the annular duct and accessory pancreatic duct. In patients who are symptomatic, treatment is surgery to relieve gastric outlet or duodenal obstruction by a bypass of the annulus. Incorrect Options: Option A - Pancreaticoduodenectomy: Pancreaticoduodenectomy or Whipple procedure may be indicated in patients with obstructive pancreatic duct stones and chronic pancreatitis or in those who have a potentially malignant periampullary lesion. Option B - Surgical resection of the annular ring: Surgical resection is associated with pancreatitis and fistula formation, without complete relief of the obstruction. Option C - Biliary stent: Biliary stenting is not indicated for the management of annular pancreas in the absence of obstructive jaundice @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Gaucher disease: Gaucher disease is a rare genetic disorder caused by the deficiency of an enzyme called glucocerebrosidase, leading to the accumulation of a substance called glucocerebroside in cells, particularly macrophages. This buildup can cause enlargement of the spleen (splenomegaly) and may result in symptoms like fatigue, weakness, and a feeling of fullness in the abdomen due to the enlarged spleen. Laboratory findings can include anemia and thrombocytopenia due to the sequestration of blood cells in the spleen. Incorrect Options: Option A - Rheumatoid arthritis: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disorder primarily affecting the joints. It typically does not cause symptoms like fatigue, weakness, or splenomegaly (enlarged spleen). Laboratory findings in rheumatoid arthritis are more focused on autoimmune markers and inflammatory markers rather than anemia and thrombocytopenia. Option B - Infectious mononucleosis (EBV): Infectious mononucleosis, caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, and splenomegaly. On examination, it is found that his jugular venous pressure (JVP) is high. The JVP is 12 cm above the angle of the sternum. questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old man comes to the emergency department with breathlessness and swollen legs. He has a history of heart failure. On examination, it is found that his jugular venous pressure (JVP) is high. The JVP is 12 cm above the angle of the sternum. Which of the following findings is most likely to be present on further examination of this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Crackles on lung auscultation: Elevated JVP, also known as jugular venous distension (JVD), is a clinical sign of increased pressure in the right atrium, which can be caused by various conditions, including heart failure, pulmonary embolism, and constrictive pericarditis. A JVP of greater than 8 cm above the sternal angle is considered abnormal. Breathlessness and leg oedema are typical signs of heart failure caused by the inability of the heart to pump enough blood to maintain circulation. Fluid can build in the lungs, creating pulmonary oedema, and patients might present with difficulty breathing, as in this example. Crackles on lung auscultation can be caused by pulmonary oedema. Crackles are discontinuous, nonmusical sounds heard during inspiration and caused by the movement of fluid or air through small airways or alveoli that are partially filled with fluid. The presence of crackles on lung auscultation in a patient with elevated JVP suggests that the patient has developed pulmonary oedema, which is a serious complication of heart failure that requires immediate medical attention. The accumulation of fluid in the lungs can impair gas exchange and lead to respiratory distress, hypoxia, and respiratory failure. Prompt recognition and management of pulmonary oedema are critical to improving patient outcomes and preventing complications. Treatment for pulmonary oedema typically includes oxygen therapy, diuretics, and medications to improve heart function, such as ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hypotension: Hypotension is less likely to be present in this patient, as the elevated JVP suggests that there is still adequate filling pressure in the heart. However, if the heart failure is severe enough, hypotension can occur. Moreover, in heart failure, the compensatory mechanisms can lead to an increase in sympathetic activity, which can raise the heart rate and peripheral vascular resistance, thereby maintaining or increasing blood pressure. Option C- Tachycardia: Tachycardia is a nonspecific finding that can be present in many conditions, including heart failure. However, it is not as specific to heart failure as crackles on lung auscultation. Option D- Normal blood pressure: Normal blood pressure is less likely to be present in this patient, as heart failure can lead to elevated blood pressure due to increased sympathetic activity. His PaO2 on room air is 65 mm Hg. In addition to treatment for community acquired pneumonia, which of the following therapies should be initiated in the ED?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Oral corticosteroids: Oral corticosteroids In cases of HIV-positive patients presenting with pneumonia, particularly those with a low CD4 count, oral corticosteroids are an important component of treatment in addition to antimicrobial therapy. Steroids help to reduce the inflammatory response and improve lung function. They are especially useful in cases where there is significant hypoxemia, as in this patient with a PaO2 of 65 mm Hg on room air. The most common cause of pneumonia in patients with HIV is Streptococcus pneumoniae. Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly carinii) is the most common opportunistic infection in AIDS patients and classically affects those with a CD4 count less than 200 cells/mL. Clinical presentation and chest X-ray findings are not highly sensitive for PJP cases, so patients are often treated empirically, particularly when they are hypoxic upon presentation. TMP-SMX is the treatment of choice for PJP, and has been shown to be superior to other antimicrobials. Anti-retroviral therapy should be started within 2 weeks of diagnosis of an opportunistic infection in order to prevent progression of AIDS and death. Treatment does not need to be started while in the ED. Incorrect Options: Option A - Aerosolized pentamidine: Aersolized pentamidine should not be used to treat PJP. It has limited efficacy and is associated with frequent relapses. Option C - Immediate initiation of anti-retroviral therapy: Anti-retroviral therapy should be started within 2 weeks of diagnosis of an opportunistic infection in order to prevent progression of AIDS and death. Treatment does not need to be started while in the ED. Option D - Parenteral amphotericin B: Parenteral amphotericin B is used in cases of severe fungal infections, and its use is not indicated for the initial treatment of community-acquired pneumonia in an HIV-positive patient @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient presents with fatigue, easy bruising, and recurrent infections. Physical examination reveals splenomegaly. Laboratory tests show decreased levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Bone marrow biopsy indicates compensatory hyperplasia. Which of the following conditions best explains the clinical presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old patient presents with fatigue, easy bruising, and recurrent infections. Physical examination reveals splenomegaly. Laboratory tests show decreased levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Bone marrow biopsy indicates compensatory hyperplasia. Which of the following conditions best explains the clinical presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Hypersplenism: Hypersplenism occurs when the spleen becomes overactive and removes blood cells (red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets) from the circulation at an accelerated rate. This can lead to decreased levels of all three types of blood cells, resulting in fatigue, easy bruising, and increased susceptibility to infections. The enlarged spleen (splenomegaly) is a characteristic finding in hypersplenism. Compensatory hyperplasia of the bone marrow occurs in response to the increased demand for blood cell production. This condition fits well with the patient's clinical presentation. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hemolytic anemia: Hemolytic anemia is characterized by the destruction of red blood cells, leading to decreased levels of red blood cells and the presence of symptoms like fatigue and easy bruising. However, the presentation in the question mentions decreased levels of white blood cells and platelets as well, which is not typical of hemolytic anemia. Additionally, compensatory hyperplasia of the bone marrow is not commonly associated with hemolytic anemia. Option B – Hemophilia: Hemophilia is a genetic disorder that primarily affects blood clotting factors, leading to prolonged bleeding and easy bruising. While it can present with easy bruising and bleeding, it does not explain the decreased levels of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, nor does it cause splenomegaly or bone marrow hyperplasia. Option D - Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP): TTP is a rare disorder characterized by microvascular thrombosis, resulting in low platelet levels (thrombocytopenia) and widespread small blood vessel damage. It can lead to symptoms such as easy bruising and bleeding, but it typically presents with features like fever, neurological symptoms, and schistocytes (fragmented red blood cells) on blood smear. While TTP can cause thrombocytopenia, it does not explain the decreased levels of red and white blood cells, nor does it commonly cause splenomegaly or bone marrow hyperplasia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 34-year-old 8 month pregnant lady presents in the medical emergency room with acute onset chest pain for the last 6 hours and associated shortness of breath. Pain is limited to the anterior chest and is pleuritic and positional, worsening in the recumbent position. There is a history of recent self-limiting gastroenteritis 1 week back. Examination reveals normal vital signs with a pericardial friction rub at the left sternal border. ECG shows diffuse ST-elevation with reciprocal depression in lead aVR and V1. CRP and WBC count are raised. She has no history of such an event in the past. Considering the likely possibility, which of the following drug should be started?
questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old 8 month pregnant lady presents in the medical emergency room with acute onset chest pain for the last 6 hours and associated shortness of breath. Pain is limited to the anterior chest and is pleuritic and positional, worsening in the recumbent position. There is a history of recent self-limiting gastroenteritis 1 week back. Examination reveals normal vital signs with a pericardial friction rub at the left sternal border. ECG shows diffuse ST-elevation with reciprocal depression in lead aVR and V1. CRP and WBC count are raised. She has no history of such an event in the past. Considering the likely possibility, which of the following drug should be started?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Colchicine: The clinical scenario and physical findings are classical of acute pericarditis secondary to viral infection, and the drug of choice for this pregnant lady is colchicine. Acute viral or idiopathic pericarditis is a self-limiting disease of the pericardium. Non-specific and only symptomatic treatment are all that is needed for medical management of uncomplicated pericardial effusion. The first line drug in acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), i.e. aspirin or ibuprofen with or without colchicine. NSAIDs are contraindicated in pregnancy, especially in the last trimester, as is this lady, therefore the first-line treatment option for this lady is to start with colchicine. Colchicine should be continued for 3 months at a dose of 0.5mg-0.6mg orally twice daily for individuals with >70kg weight and once daily for individuals with <70kg weight. Colchicine blocks the assembly of microtubules in WBCs, thereby exerting its anti-inflammatory effects. Colchicine, especially when used with NSAIDs, is well tolerated, alleviates symptoms and decreases the incidence of recurrence. Colchicine is not approved for pyogenic and malignancy-related pericarditis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Ibuprofen: Ibuprofen is not the right agent here as it is contraindicated in pregnancy of >20 weeks. Although NSAIDs are the first-line agent for treating idiopathic and viral pericarditis but are not safe in pregnancy. These can cause oligohydramnios and patent ductus arteriosus. Option C - Prednisolone: Prednisolone is not the right option to start with in this patient. Steroids are indicated for treating recurrent pericarditis or initial-treatment failure with NSAIDs or colchicine. As this patient presents with the first episode of pericarditis with no previous treatment exposure, this is not the right drug to start. Option D - Acyclovir: Acyclovir is not the right treatment for this patient. Antiviral therapy is not recommended for treating viral pericarditis as it is a self-limiting disease. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man, who is a keen rambler and gardener, comes to a multi-disciplinary MSK clinic with painful knees. His pain is worse on activity, particularly coming down slopes and when kneeling. He complains of a few minutes of stiffness after sitting for any length of time and in the mornings. He has never suffered from locking or giving way. No other joints are affected. On occasion, he has taken his wife's Voltarol for the pain but takes nothing regularly. His x-rays show tricompartmental joint narrowing and subchondral cyst formation. Which treatment would you advise?
questions.stemHtml:
A 54-year-old man, who is a keen rambler and gardener, comes to a multi-disciplinary MSK clinic with painful knees. His pain is worse on activity, particularly coming down slopes and when kneeling. He complains of a few minutes of stiffness after sitting for any length of time and in the mornings. He has never suffered from locking or giving way. No other joints are affected. On occasion, he has taken his wife's Voltarol for the pain but takes nothing regularly. His x-rays show tricompartmental joint narrowing and subchondral cyst formation.
Which treatment would you advise?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Paracetamol: This gentleman is reporting symptoms of knee osteoarthritis . NICE guidelines recommend that in the first instance paracetamol should be offered and may need to be taken regularly. Since this gentleman has not used any regular medication up to this point paracetamol is the most appropriate choice. Next line would be to add a topical NSAID for those with knee and hand OA. Thereafter, an oral NSAID or cox 2 antagonist, should be co-prescribed with a PPI. Incorrect Options: Option A - Arthroscopy and lavage: Knee arthroscopy and lavage should only be recommended for those with locking or giving way, symptoms suggestive of loose bodies. Exercise, for local muscle training and general fitness, should be recommended for all patients. Only those refractory to medical management as outlined above should be referred for surgery, but referral should be made before there is prolonged and established functional limitation and severe pain. Option C - Glucosamine and chondroitin: Glucosamine and chondroitin are commonly used as supplements to help manage symptoms of osteoarthritis. However, their effectiveness in treating knee osteoarthritis is a subject of debate, and evidence supporting their use is not very strong. Some studies have shown modest benefits in pain relief, while others have not found significant effects. In this case, the patient's symptoms are moderate, and there are more effective treatment options available. Option D - Methotrexate: Methotrexate is a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) commonly used in the treatment of inflammatory types of arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis. It works by suppressing the immune system to reduce inflammation. However, in this case, the patient's symptoms are consistent with osteoarthritis, which is a degenerative joint disease rather than an inflammatory condition. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Decreasing the Activity of Aminolevulinic Acid Synthase: This patient has a clinical scenario that would be consistent with AIP. Aminolevulinic Acid Synthase is an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of succinyl-CoA and glycine to ALA, the first and rate-limiting step in heme synthesis. Decreasing the activity of aminolevulinic acid synthase is a therapeutic approach in treating AIP because it reduces the accumulation of ALA, which subsequently decreases the production of porphobilinogen and other porphyrin precursors, helping to alleviate the symptoms of porphyria. Increasing the activity of the enzyme that's already deficient would not address the underlying problem of porphyrin precursor accumulation. Option D - Decreased Targeting of Heme Degradation by the Adaptive Immune System: Similar to the first incorrect choice, this option doesn't accurately reflect the mechanism of action of medications used to treat porphyria.
